Atrial Fibrillation (AFib).education:
What is Atrial Fibrillation (AFib)?
Atrial fibrillation (AFib) is a common heart rhythm disorder in which the upper chambers of the heart (atria) beat irregularly and often too fast. Instead of the heart's electrical signals firing in a coordinated pattern, multiple signals fire at once, causing the atria to quiver rather than contract effectively. This irregular rhythm reduces the heart's ability to pump blood efficiently and allows blood to pool in the atria, which significantly increases the risk of blood clots forming. If a clot travels to the brain, it can cause a stroke. AFib also increases the risk of heart failure and other cardiovascular complications over time. AFib may occur in episodes that come and go (paroxysmal), may persist for longer periods (persistent), or may become a permanent condition. Some people experience AFib without any noticeable symptoms, making regular check-ups and pulse monitoring important. Treatment focuses on controlling the heart rate or rhythm, preventing blood clots with anticoagulant medications, and managing underlying conditions such as high blood pressure, heart valve disease, and thyroid disorders.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Rapid or irregular heartbeat (palpitations)
•Fluttering or pounding sensation in the chest
•Dizziness or lightheadedness
•Fatigue or weakness
•Shortness of breath, especially with activity
•Chest pain or discomfort
•Reduced ability to exercise
•Confusion
•Some people may have no noticeable symptoms

Risk Factors:
•Older age
•High blood pressure
•Heart valve disease
•Coronary artery disease or prior heart attack
•Heart failure
•Obesity
•Diabetes
•Hyperthyroidism
•Sleep apnea
•Chronic lung disease
•Excessive alcohol or caffeine intake
•Family history of AFib
•Prior heart surgery

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take all prescribed medications exactly as directed, including blood thinners (anticoagulants), rate-control, or rhythm-control medications.
•Do not stop or change medications without consulting the healthcare provider.
•Monitor pulse regularly as directed by the healthcare provider.
•Keep all scheduled cardiology and PCP appointments.
•Limit or avoid alcohol and caffeine as recommended.
•Maintain a healthy weight.
•Stay physically active as tolerated and approved by the healthcare provider.
•Manage stress through relaxation techniques, exercise, or counseling.
•Report new or worsening palpitations, dizziness, fainting, shortness of breath, or chest pain to the healthcare provider promptly.

Congestive Heart Failure.education:
What is Congestive Heart Failure (CHF)?
Congestive heart failure is a chronic, progressive condition in which the heart muscle does not pump blood as effectively as it should. When the heart's pumping action is weakened, blood and fluid can back up into the lungs, abdomen, liver, and lower extremities, causing congestion. CHF can result from conditions that damage or overwork the heart over time, such as coronary artery disease, heart attack, high blood pressure, heart valve disease, cardiomyopathy, or chronic arrhythmias. The heart may become too weak to pump enough blood forward (systolic heart failure) or too stiff to fill properly between beats (diastolic heart failure). As the heart struggles to keep up with demand, the body compensates by retaining sodium and water, which leads to fluid overload and worsening symptoms. Without proper management, CHF can progressively worsen and lead to frequent hospitalizations. Managing CHF requires a combination of daily self-monitoring — including daily weights, tracking fluid intake, and recognizing warning signs — along with taking prescribed medications consistently, following a low-sodium diet, staying physically active as tolerated, and attending regular follow-up appointments.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Shortness of breath, especially with activity or when lying flat
•Persistent coughing or wheezing, sometimes producing white or pink-tinged mucus
•Swelling (edema) of the feet, ankles, legs, or abdomen
•Fatigue or weakness
•Rapid or irregular heartbeat
•Reduced ability to exercise
•Increased need to urinate at night
•Sudden weight gain from fluid retention
•Difficulty concentrating or decreased alertness
•Nausea or loss of appetite

Risk Factors:
•Coronary artery disease or prior heart attack
•High blood pressure
•Diabetes
•Obesity
•Heart valve disease
•Cardiomyopathy or family history of cardiomyopathy
•History of myocarditis
•Congenital heart defects
•Chronic lung disease
•Sleep apnea
•Excessive alcohol use
•Tobacco use
•Older age

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take all prescribed medications exactly as directed, including ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, diuretics, or other heart failure medications.
•Do not stop or change medications without consulting the healthcare provider.
•Weigh yourself daily at the same time, wearing similar clothing, and record the weight.
•Report weight gain of more than 2-3 pounds in one day or 5 pounds in one week to the healthcare provider.
•Limit sodium intake as directed by the healthcare provider.
•Limit fluid intake if directed by the healthcare provider.
•Stay physically active as tolerated and approved by the healthcare provider.
•Elevate legs when sitting to reduce swelling.
•Get adequate rest and avoid overexertion.
•Keep all scheduled cardiology and PCP appointments.
•Receive recommended vaccinations, including influenza and pneumococcal vaccines.
•Avoid tobacco and limit alcohol as directed.

Coronary Artery Disease.education:
What is Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)?
Coronary artery disease (CAD) is a condition in which the arteries that supply blood and oxygen to the heart become narrowed or blocked due to the buildup of cholesterol and fatty deposits called plaque (atherosclerosis). Over time, this reduces blood flow to the heart and can increase the risk of chest pain (angina), heart attack, heart failure, and stroke. High blood pressure places extra strain on the heart and blood vessels, while high cholesterol contributes directly to plaque buildup in the arteries. Diabetes accelerates atherosclerosis, and smoking damages the lining of blood vessels, making plaque accumulation worse. CAD develops gradually over many years and may not produce symptoms until the arteries are significantly narrowed or a sudden blockage occurs. A heart attack happens when a plaque ruptures and a blood clot forms, completely blocking blood flow to part of the heart muscle. Managing CAD requires a comprehensive approach including taking medications as prescribed, following a heart-healthy diet low in saturated fat and sodium, engaging in regular physical activity as tolerated, maintaining a healthy weight, avoiding tobacco use, controlling blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar levels, and promptly reporting symptoms such as chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness, fainting, or swelling to a healthcare provider.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Chest pain or pressure (angina), especially with activity or stress
•Shortness of breath
•Fatigue or weakness
•Dizziness or lightheadedness
•Palpitations or irregular heartbeat
•Nausea
•Pain radiating to the arm, shoulder, neck, jaw, or back
•Some people may have no symptoms until a heart attack occurs

Risk Factors:
•High blood pressure
•High cholesterol (dyslipidemia)
•Diabetes
•Smoking or tobacco use
•Overweight or obesity
•Physical inactivity
•Unhealthy diet high in saturated fat, trans fat, cholesterol, and sodium
•Family history of heart disease
•Older age
•Chronic stress
•Excessive alcohol consumption

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed medications exactly as directed, including cholesterol-lowering, blood pressure, antiplatelet, and other cardiac medications.
•Do not stop or change medications without consulting the healthcare provider.
•Follow a heart-healthy diet low in saturated fat, cholesterol, and sodium.
•Engage in regular physical activity as tolerated and approved by the healthcare provider.
•Maintain a healthy weight.
•Stop smoking and avoid secondhand smoke.
•Manage stress through healthy coping strategies.
•Monitor blood pressure and cholesterol levels as recommended.
•Keep all scheduled cardiology and PCP appointments.
•Report chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness, fainting, or swelling to the healthcare provider promptly.

Dyslipidemia.education:
What is Dyslipidemia?
Dyslipidemia refers to unhealthy levels of cholesterol and/or other fats (lipids) in the blood. This includes elevated LDL ("bad") cholesterol, elevated triglycerides, and/or low HDL ("good") cholesterol. High LDL cholesterol is a major contributor to atherosclerosis — the buildup of plaque inside the arteries — which narrows and hardens blood vessels over time, restricting blood flow to the heart, brain, and other organs. This process significantly increases the risk of heart attack, stroke, and peripheral artery disease. Dyslipidemia usually does not cause any noticeable symptoms, which is why routine blood tests (lipid panels) are essential for early detection and ongoing monitoring. Many people are unaware they have high cholesterol until a cardiovascular event occurs. Dyslipidemia can be caused by genetic factors (familial hypercholesterolemia), lifestyle factors such as a diet high in saturated fat and physical inactivity, or other medical conditions including diabetes, hypothyroidism, kidney disease, and liver disease. Treatment typically involves a combination of lifestyle modifications — heart-healthy eating, regular exercise, weight management, and smoking cessation — along with cholesterol-lowering medications such as statins when indicated.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Dyslipidemia often has no noticeable symptoms
•Very high cholesterol levels may sometimes cause yellowish deposits under the skin (xanthomas)
•Whitish ring around the cornea of the eye (arcus cornealis)
•Symptoms may not appear until a cardiovascular event such as heart attack or stroke occurs
•Routine blood tests (lipid panel) are the primary way to detect dyslipidemia

•Family history of high cholesterol or heart disease
•Diet high in saturated fat, trans fat, and cholesterol

•Physical inactivity

•Engage in regular physical activity as tolerated and approved by the healthcare provider.

Hypertension.education:
What is Hypertension?
Hypertension (high blood pressure) occurs when the force of blood pushing against the walls of the blood vessels is consistently too high. Blood pressure is recorded as two numbers: systolic pressure (the top number, measuring pressure when the heart beats) and diastolic pressure (the bottom number, measuring pressure when the heart rests between beats). Normal blood pressure is generally below 120/80 mm Hg. Hypertension is often called the "silent killer" because it typically causes no symptoms, even when blood pressure levels are dangerously high. Over time, uncontrolled high blood pressure damages blood vessels throughout the body and forces the heart to work harder, significantly increasing the risk of heart attack, stroke, heart failure, kidney disease, vision loss, and other serious health problems. Contributing factors include genetics, a diet high in sodium, lack of regular physical activity, excess body weight, chronic stress, smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, sleep apnea, and certain chronic conditions such as diabetes and kidney disease. Managing hypertension requires consistent effort, including taking blood pressure medications exactly as prescribed, monitoring blood pressure regularly at home, following a low-sodium diet such as the DASH eating plan, staying physically active, maintaining a healthy weight, limiting alcohol, avoiding tobacco, managing stress, and keeping all follow-up appointments with the healthcare provider.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Hypertension often has no noticeable symptoms
•Very high blood pressure may sometimes be associated with:
  •Severe headache
  •Dizziness
  •Vision changes or blurred vision
  •Chest pain
  •Shortness of breath
  •Nosebleeds
  •Blood in the urine
•Regular blood pressure checks are important even when feeling well

Risk Factors:
•Family history of high blood pressure or heart disease
•Older age
•Being overweight or obese
•Lack of regular physical activity
•Diet high in sodium (salt)
•Excessive alcohol intake
•Tobacco use or exposure to secondhand smoke
•Chronic stress
•Poor sleep or sleep apnea
•Diabetes
•Kidney disease
•Certain medications

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take blood pressure medications exactly as prescribed.
•Do not stop or change medications without consulting the healthcare provider.
•Check and record blood pressure at home as directed.
•Sit quietly for at least 5 minutes before taking a reading.
•Keep feet flat on the floor and support the arm at heart level during measurement.
•Bring blood pressure readings to healthcare appointments.
•Notify the healthcare provider if readings are repeatedly outside the recommended range.
•Maintain a healthy weight.
•Avoid tobacco products and secondhand smoke.
•Limit alcohol as recommended.
•Participate in regular physical activity as tolerated and approved by the healthcare provider.
•Manage stress through relaxation techniques, exercise, hobbies, or counseling.
•Keep all scheduled PCP and cardiology appointments.

Sick Sinus Syndrome.education:
What is Sick Sinus Syndrome (SSS)?
Sick sinus syndrome is a group of heart rhythm disorders in which the heart's natural pacemaker (the sinus node) does not function properly. The sinus node, located in the right atrium, generates the electrical impulses that control the heartbeat. When it malfunctions, the heart may beat too slowly (bradycardia), too fast (tachycardia), or alternate between slow and fast rhythms (tachy-brady syndrome). This can cause inadequate blood flow to the brain and body, leading to symptoms such as dizziness, fainting, fatigue, and shortness of breath. Sick sinus syndrome is most common in older adults and may be caused by age-related degeneration of the heart's electrical system, prior heart surgery, heart disease, or certain medications. Many people with sick sinus syndrome require a permanent pacemaker to maintain an adequate heart rate. In addition to pacemaker management, treatment may include medications to control heart rhythm and blood thinners to reduce the risk of blood clots and stroke.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Dizziness or lightheadedness
•Fainting or near-fainting (syncope)
•Fatigue or weakness
•Shortness of breath
•Palpitations or feeling the heart racing or fluttering
•Chest discomfort
•Confusion or difficulty concentrating
•Pauses in heartbeat
•Some people may have no symptoms

Risk Factors:
•Older age
•History of heart disease or prior heart surgery
•High blood pressure
•Heart valve disease
•Cardiomyopathy
•Myocarditis (inflammation of the heart)
•Medications that slow heart rate
•Congenital heart defects
•Infiltrative diseases affecting the heart

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Keep all scheduled cardiology and pacemaker/device-check appointments.
•Carry the pacemaker identification card and consider wearing medical identification if a pacemaker is implanted.
•Inform healthcare providers, dentists, and other medical professionals about the pacemaker.
•Follow the cardiologist's recommendations regarding physical activity and exercise.
•Check the pacemaker incision/site as directed and report redness, swelling, warmth, drainage, worsening pain, or fever.
•Do not place strong magnets directly over the pacemaker.
•Follow the pacemaker manufacturer's and cardiologist's instructions regarding cell phones, headphones, security systems, and other electronic devices.
•Discuss MRI scans or procedures involving electrical equipment with the healthcare provider before they are performed.
•Take all prescribed medications as directed.
•Report dizziness, fainting, unusual weakness, worsening shortness of breath, or new palpitations to the healthcare provider.

Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm.education:
What is an Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)?
An abdominal aortic aneurysm is an abnormal enlargement or bulging of the aorta, the largest blood vessel in the body, as it passes through the abdomen. The aorta carries blood from the heart to the rest of the body. When the wall of the aorta weakens, it can balloon outward and continue to grow over time. If an aneurysm grows too large or expands too rapidly, it can rupture, which is a life-threatening medical emergency with a high mortality rate. Most small aneurysms grow slowly and may never rupture, but they require regular monitoring with imaging to track their size. Aneurysms larger than 5.5 centimeters or those growing rapidly may require surgical repair, either through open surgery or endovascular stent-graft placement. The greatest risk factor for AAA is smoking, which damages the walls of blood vessels. Other contributing factors include high blood pressure, atherosclerosis, family history, older age, and male sex. Managing an AAA involves controlling blood pressure and cholesterol, quitting smoking, attending all surveillance appointments, and knowing when to seek emergency care.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Most small AAAs cause no symptoms and are found incidentally during imaging
•Deep, constant pain in the abdomen or side of the abdomen
•Back pain
•Pulsating feeling near the navel
•A ruptured AAA causes sudden, severe abdominal or back pain, dizziness, rapid heartbeat, and loss of consciousness

Risk Factors:
•Smoking (strongest risk factor)
•Male sex
•Age 65 or older
•Family history of aortic aneurysm
•High blood pressure
•Atherosclerosis (hardening of the arteries)
•History of other aneurysms
•Connective tissue disorders

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Attend all scheduled follow-up imaging and appointments to monitor aneurysm size.
•Take blood pressure and cholesterol medications as prescribed.
•Stop smoking and avoid all tobacco products.
•Maintain blood pressure within the provider-recommended range.
•Engage in moderate physical activity as approved by the healthcare provider.
•Avoid heavy lifting or straining as directed.
•Report new or worsening abdominal or back pain immediately.
•Notify the healthcare provider of any new pulsating sensation in the abdomen.

PAD.education:
What is Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD)?
Peripheral arterial disease is a common circulatory condition in which narrowed or blocked arteries reduce blood flow to the limbs, most commonly the legs. PAD is caused primarily by atherosclerosis — the same process of plaque buildup that causes coronary artery disease and stroke. When the arteries supplying the legs become narrowed, the muscles do not receive enough blood during activity, which causes cramping pain (claudication). As the disease progresses, blood flow may become insufficient even at rest, leading to critical limb ischemia, non-healing wounds, tissue death (gangrene), and in severe cases, the need for amputation. PAD is a strong indicator of widespread atherosclerosis, meaning people with PAD are at significantly higher risk for heart attack and stroke. Many people with PAD have no symptoms or attribute their leg pain to aging, which is why screening is important for at-risk individuals. Treatment involves aggressive management of cardiovascular risk factors — quitting smoking, controlling blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar, taking prescribed medications including antiplatelet agents, and participating in a supervised walking program to improve circulation and reduce symptoms.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Leg pain or cramping during walking or exercise that improves with rest (claudication)
•Numbness, tingling, or weakness in the legs
•Coldness in the lower leg or foot compared to the other side
•Sores or wounds on the toes, feet, or legs that heal slowly or do not heal
•Color changes in the skin of the legs or feet
•Shiny skin on the legs
•Decreased or absent pulse in the feet
•Erectile dysfunction in men
•Some people may have no symptoms

Risk Factors:
•Smoking (strongest risk factor)
•Diabetes
•High blood pressure
•High cholesterol
•Older age (especially over 50)
•Family history of PAD, heart disease, or stroke
•Obesity
•Physical inactivity
•Kidney disease

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take all prescribed medications as directed, including antiplatelet, cholesterol, and blood pressure medications.
•Stop smoking and avoid all tobacco products.
•Walk regularly as prescribed by the healthcare provider to improve circulation and reduce symptoms.
•Inspect feet and legs daily for cuts, sores, blisters, redness, or skin changes.
•Keep feet clean, dry, and moisturized.
•Wear properly fitting shoes and protective footwear.
•Do not walk barefoot.
•Manage blood sugar, blood pressure, and cholesterol levels as directed.
•Keep all scheduled vascular and PCP appointments.
•Report new or worsening leg pain, non-healing wounds, or skin color changes promptly.

PVD.education:
What is Peripheral Vascular Disease (PVD)?
Peripheral vascular disease is a broad term for diseases affecting blood vessels outside the heart and brain, most commonly in the legs. PVD encompasses conditions of both the arteries (peripheral arterial disease) and the veins (chronic venous insufficiency, deep vein thrombosis). Arterial PVD is caused by atherosclerosis and reduces blood supply to the extremities, while venous PVD involves problems with blood return to the heart, leading to pooling, swelling, and skin changes. Both forms can significantly affect mobility, wound healing, and quality of life. Arterial PVD carries the same cardiovascular risks as PAD, including increased risk of heart attack and stroke. Venous PVD can lead to chronic leg swelling, skin discoloration, venous ulcers, and blood clots. Risk factors for PVD include smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, obesity, physical inactivity, and older age. Treatment depends on the type and severity and may include medications, compression therapy for venous disease, exercise programs, lifestyle modifications, and in some cases, surgical or endovascular procedures.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Pain, aching, or cramping in the legs during walking or activity
•Numbness, tingling, or weakness in the legs or feet
•Coldness in the lower legs or feet
•Color changes in the skin (pale, bluish, or reddish)
•Slow-healing sores or wounds on the legs or feet
•Swelling of the legs or ankles (venous disease)
•Varicose veins or skin changes from chronic venous insufficiency
•Reduced hair growth on the legs
•Weak or absent pulses in the legs or feet

Risk Factors:
•Smoking
•Diabetes
•High blood pressure
•High cholesterol
•Older age
•Obesity
•Physical inactivity
•Family history of vascular disease
•History of blood clots

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take all prescribed medications as directed.
•Stop smoking and avoid tobacco products.
•Walk and exercise regularly as approved by the healthcare provider.
•Inspect feet and legs daily for cuts, sores, or changes.
•Keep feet clean, dry, and moisturized.
•Wear compression stockings if prescribed for venous disease.
•Elevate legs when sitting to reduce swelling if directed.
•Manage blood sugar, blood pressure, and cholesterol as directed.
•Avoid prolonged sitting or standing without movement.
•Keep all scheduled appointments with the vascular specialist and PCP.
•Report worsening pain, swelling, skin changes, or non-healing wounds.

Asthma.education:
What is Asthma?
Asthma is a chronic respiratory condition that causes inflammation, swelling, and narrowing of the airways (bronchial tubes) in the lungs. During an asthma episode, the muscles around the airways tighten (bronchospasm), the airway lining becomes swollen and inflamed, and excess mucus is produced, all of which restrict airflow and make breathing difficult. Asthma symptoms can range from mild to severe and may vary over time. Triggers that provoke asthma symptoms differ from person to person and can include allergens (dust mites, pollen, pet dander, mold), respiratory infections, exercise, cold air, smoke, air pollution, strong odors, stress, and certain medications. Asthma cannot be cured, but with proper treatment and an individualized asthma action plan, most people with asthma can control their symptoms and live active lives. Treatment typically includes two types of medications: long-term controller medications taken daily to reduce airway inflammation and prevent symptoms, and quick-relief (rescue) medications used to rapidly open the airways during an asthma attack. Recognizing early warning signs and knowing how to respond is critical to preventing severe episodes and emergency department visits.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Shortness of breath
•Wheezing
•Coughing, especially at night or early in the morning
•Chest tightness
•Difficulty breathing
•Symptoms that worsen with exercise, illness, allergies, smoke, or other triggers

Risk Factors:
•Family history of asthma or allergies
•Personal history of allergies (allergic rhinitis, eczema)
•Respiratory infections in childhood
•Exposure to secondhand smoke
•Exposure to air pollution, dust, mold, or chemical fumes
•Obesity
•Occupational exposure to irritants

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take asthma medications exactly as prescribed.
•Use daily controller medication consistently if prescribed.
•Keep the prescribed quick-relief/rescue inhaler readily available at all times.
•Know the difference between controller and rescue medications.
•Use the correct inhaler technique and spacer if prescribed.
•Do not stop or change medications without consulting the healthcare provider.
•Notify the healthcare provider if the rescue inhaler is needed more frequently than usual.
•Identify and avoid known asthma triggers.
•Follow the individualized asthma action plan provided by the healthcare provider.
•Receive recommended vaccinations, including influenza and COVID-19.
•Keep all scheduled PCP and pulmonology appointments.

COPD.education:
What is Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)?
COPD is a chronic, progressive lung disease that causes persistent airflow obstruction, making it increasingly difficult to breathe. COPD encompasses two main conditions: chronic bronchitis (long-term inflammation of the airways with excess mucus production) and emphysema (destruction of the air sacs where oxygen exchange occurs). Most people with COPD have features of both. The primary cause of COPD is long-term exposure to lung irritants, with cigarette smoking being responsible for the vast majority of cases. Occupational dust, chemical fumes, air pollution, and the genetic condition alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency can also cause COPD. The damage to the lungs is permanent and worsens over time, but treatment can slow the progression, reduce symptoms, decrease the frequency and severity of flare-ups (exacerbations), and improve quality of life. COPD exacerbations — episodes of acutely worsened symptoms often triggered by respiratory infections — are a leading cause of hospitalization and can accelerate lung function decline. Management includes quitting smoking, using prescribed inhaler medications consistently, participating in pulmonary rehabilitation, receiving recommended vaccinations, maintaining good nutrition, and learning breathing techniques to manage shortness of breath.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Shortness of breath, especially with activity
•Chronic cough
•Increased mucus (phlegm) production
•Wheezing
•Chest tightness
•Fatigue
•Frequent respiratory infections
•Difficulty taking deep breaths
•Bluish lips or fingernails (cyanosis) in severe cases
•Swelling of the ankles, feet, or legs in advanced disease

Risk Factors:
•Smoking or history of smoking
•Exposure to secondhand smoke
•Long-term exposure to air pollution
•Occupational exposure to dust, fumes, or chemicals
•Older age
•History of asthma
•Family history of COPD or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
•Frequent respiratory infections
•Poor air quality or biomass fuel exposure

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Stop smoking and avoid exposure to lung irritants.
•Take prescribed inhalers and medications as directed.
•Use supplemental oxygen if prescribed.
•Participate in pulmonary rehabilitation if recommended.
•Stay physically active as tolerated.
•Practice breathing techniques, such as pursed-lip and diaphragmatic breathing.
•Receive recommended vaccinations, including influenza, COVID-19, and pneumococcal vaccines.
•Maintain good nutrition and adequate hydration.
•Seek prompt treatment for respiratory infections.
•Attend regular follow-up appointments with the PCP and pulmonologist.

Cystic Fibrosis.education:
What is Cystic Fibrosis (CF)?
Cystic fibrosis is a serious, inherited genetic disorder that affects the cells that produce mucus, sweat, and digestive fluids. In people with CF, a defective gene causes these secretions to become abnormally thick and sticky instead of thin and slippery. The thick mucus clogs the airways in the lungs, trapping bacteria and leading to repeated, severe lung infections that progressively damage the lungs. CF also blocks the ducts of the pancreas, preventing digestive enzymes from reaching the intestines, which impairs the digestion and absorption of nutrients — particularly fats and fat-soluble vitamins. Over time, chronic lung infections and inflammation can lead to permanent lung damage, respiratory failure, and the need for lung transplantation. CF is a lifelong condition, but advances in treatment — particularly CFTR modulator therapies that address the underlying protein defect — have significantly improved life expectancy and quality of life. Daily management of CF is intensive and includes airway clearance techniques, inhaled medications, pancreatic enzyme replacement with all meals and snacks, nutritional supplementation, regular exercise, and vigilant infection prevention.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Persistent cough that produces thick mucus
•Frequent lung infections such as pneumonia and bronchitis
•Wheezing or shortness of breath
•Poor growth or weight gain despite good appetite
•Very salty-tasting skin
•Frequent, greasy, or bulky stools
•Difficulty with bowel movements or intestinal blockage
•Nasal polyps or chronic sinus infections
•Clubbing of the fingers and toes
•Male infertility

Risk Factors:
•Family history of cystic fibrosis (inherited genetic condition)
•Both parents must carry the CF gene mutation
•Most commonly affects Caucasian individuals

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take all prescribed medications as directed, including CFTR modulators, mucus-thinning medications, bronchodilators, and antibiotics.
•Perform airway clearance techniques daily as directed.
•Take pancreatic enzyme replacements with meals and snacks as prescribed.
•Take prescribed vitamins and nutritional supplements.
•Maintain a high-calorie, high-fat diet as recommended.
•Stay physically active as tolerated.
•Avoid exposure to cigarette smoke, air pollution, and people who are sick.
•Maintain good hand hygiene.
•Keep all scheduled pulmonology, gastroenterology, and CF clinic appointments.
•Receive recommended vaccinations.

OSA.education:
What is Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)?
Obstructive sleep apnea is a common and potentially serious sleep disorder in which the muscles in the back of the throat intermittently relax and collapse during sleep, repeatedly blocking or narrowing the upper airway. Each blockage can last from a few seconds to over a minute and may occur dozens or even hundreds of times per night, causing oxygen levels to drop and disrupting sleep. The brain briefly arouses the person to reopen the airway, but these micro-awakenings are so brief that the person typically does not remember them, even though they severely fragment sleep quality. Untreated OSA is associated with significant health risks, including high blood pressure, coronary artery disease, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, stroke, type 2 diabetes, depression, and motor vehicle accidents due to daytime drowsiness. The most common treatment is continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP), which delivers pressurized air through a mask to keep the airway open during sleep. Weight loss, positional therapy, oral appliances, and in some cases surgery may also be recommended. Consistent, every-night use of the prescribed PAP device is critical for effective treatment.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Loud snoring
•Gasping or choking during sleep
•Pauses in breathing while sleeping (witnessed by a bed partner)
•Waking with a dry mouth or sore throat
•Morning headaches
•Feeling tired or sleepy during the daytime
•Difficulty concentrating or memory problems
•Irritability or mood changes
•Frequent nighttime urination

Risk Factors:
•Overweight or obesity
•Large neck circumference
•Narrowed airway
•Male sex
•Older age
•Family history of sleep apnea
•Smoking
•Nasal congestion
•Use of alcohol or sedatives
•Medical conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes, or heart failure

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Use CPAP/BiPAP every time you sleep, including naps, as prescribed.
•Do not change the pressure settings unless instructed by the healthcare provider.
•Make sure the mask fits comfortably and securely.
•Clean the mask, tubing, humidifier, and other equipment according to the manufacturer's/provider's instructions.
•Replace filters, masks, tubing, and other supplies as recommended.
•Contact the healthcare provider or equipment supplier for persistent mask leaks, skin irritation, dryness, or difficulty using the device.
•Maintain a healthy weight if recommended.
•Avoid alcohol or sedating medications near bedtime unless approved by the healthcare provider.
•Sleep on your side if recommended by the sleep specialist.
•Keep regular appointments with the sleep specialist.
•Report continued excessive daytime sleepiness or morning headaches despite regular use.

Pulmonary Fibrosis.education:
What is Pulmonary Fibrosis?
Pulmonary fibrosis is a chronic, progressive lung disease in which the lung tissue becomes thickened, stiffened, and scarred (fibrosed). As scar tissue replaces healthy lung tissue, the lungs lose their ability to expand fully and transfer oxygen efficiently into the bloodstream, leading to progressively worsening shortness of breath. The cause of pulmonary fibrosis is often unknown (idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, or IPF), but it can also result from long-term exposure to environmental or occupational toxins (asbestos, silica, coal dust), certain medications (chemotherapy agents, some cardiac drugs), radiation therapy to the chest, autoimmune or connective tissue diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma), and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Once lung scarring occurs, it cannot be reversed. Treatment focuses on slowing the progression of fibrosis with antifibrotic medications (pirfenidone or nintedanib), managing symptoms, maintaining oxygen levels with supplemental oxygen when needed, preserving physical function through pulmonary rehabilitation, and in eligible patients, evaluation for lung transplantation. Early diagnosis and treatment initiation are important because the disease tends to worsen over time.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Shortness of breath, especially with activity
•Dry, persistent cough
•Fatigue and weakness
•Unexplained weight loss
•Aching muscles and joints
•Clubbing (widening and rounding) of the fingertips and toes
•Fast, shallow breathing
•Crackling sounds heard through a stethoscope

Risk Factors:
•Smoking or history of smoking
•Environmental or occupational exposure to dust, asbestos, silica, or other irritants
•Certain medications (chemotherapy, cardiac medications)
•Radiation therapy to the chest
•Autoimmune or connective tissue diseases
•Family history of pulmonary fibrosis
•Older age (usually diagnosed between 50-70)
•Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed antifibrotic medications (pirfenidone or nintedanib) as directed.
•Use supplemental oxygen if prescribed.
•Participate in pulmonary rehabilitation if recommended.
•Stay physically active as tolerated.
•Practice breathing techniques to improve oxygen exchange.
•Receive recommended vaccinations.
•Avoid smoking and exposure to lung irritants.
•Maintain good nutrition.
•Keep all scheduled pulmonology appointments.
•Report worsening shortness of breath, cough, or decreased activity tolerance.
•Discuss lung transplant evaluation with the provider if appropriate.

Diabetes.education:
What is Diabetes?
Diabetes is a chronic metabolic condition in which the body cannot properly regulate blood glucose (sugar) levels. Glucose is the body's main source of energy and comes from the food we eat. Insulin, a hormone produced by the pancreas, helps glucose enter the cells to be used for energy. In type 1 diabetes, the body's immune system attacks and destroys the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas, requiring lifelong insulin therapy. In type 2 diabetes — the most common form — the body either does not produce enough insulin or does not use it effectively (insulin resistance), causing glucose to build up in the bloodstream. Over time, persistently high blood sugar damages blood vessels and nerves throughout the body, leading to serious complications including heart disease, stroke, kidney disease (diabetic nephropathy), nerve damage (diabetic neuropathy), eye damage and vision loss (diabetic retinopathy), poor wound healing, and increased risk of infections, particularly in the feet and lower extremities. Managing diabetes requires a comprehensive approach that includes blood sugar monitoring, medication or insulin management, following a balanced meal plan with controlled carbohydrate portions, regular physical activity, weight management, routine medical check-ups, and preventive care including regular eye, kidney, and foot examinations.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Increased thirst
•Frequent urination
•Increased hunger
•Feeling tired or weak
•Blurred vision
•Unexplained weight loss
•Cuts or wounds that heal slowly
•Frequent infections
•Numbness or tingling in the hands or feet
•Some people may have no noticeable symptoms

Risk Factors:
•Family history of diabetes
•Being overweight or obese
•Physical inactivity
•Age 35 or older
•History of prediabetes or gestational diabetes
•High blood pressure or abnormal cholesterol levels
•Certain racial or ethnic groups have an increased risk

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take diabetes medications or insulin exactly as prescribed.
•Check and record blood sugar as directed by the healthcare provider.
•Follow a healthy, balanced meal plan and control carbohydrate portions.
•Limit sugary drinks, sweets, and highly processed foods.
•Eat more vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins, and high-fiber foods.
•Stay physically active as tolerated and recommended.
•Maintain a healthy weight.
•Attend routine medical appointments and complete A1C and other recommended laboratory tests.
•Check feet daily for cuts, sores, redness, swelling, or infection.
•Complete routine eye, kidney, and foot examinations as recommended.
•Do not stop or change diabetes medications without consulting the healthcare provider.

Hyperparathyroidism.education:
What is Hyperparathyroidism?
Hyperparathyroidism is a condition in which one or more of the four small parathyroid glands, located behind the thyroid gland in the neck, produce too much parathyroid hormone (PTH). PTH normally regulates calcium and phosphorus levels in the blood and bones. When PTH is overproduced, it causes calcium to be released from the bones into the blood, leading to elevated blood calcium levels (hypercalcemia). Over time, this can weaken bones and increase the risk of osteoporosis and fractures, cause kidney stones, and affect the function of the heart, muscles, and nervous system. Primary hyperparathyroidism is most commonly caused by a benign tumor (adenoma) on one of the parathyroid glands. Secondary hyperparathyroidism occurs when another condition, such as chronic kidney disease or vitamin D deficiency, causes the parathyroid glands to overcompensate. Many people with mild hyperparathyroidism have no obvious symptoms and the condition is discovered incidentally through routine blood work showing elevated calcium levels. Treatment depends on the severity and may include surgery (parathyroidectomy) for primary hyperparathyroidism, or medical management of the underlying cause for secondary hyperparathyroidism, along with monitoring bone density, kidney function, and calcium levels.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Fatigue or weakness
•Bone pain or fragile bones (osteoporosis)
•Kidney stones
•Frequent urination and excessive thirst
•Abdominal pain, nausea, or constipation
•Depression, confusion, or difficulty concentrating
•Muscle aches or cramps
•Joint pain
•Loss of appetite
•Some people may have no noticeable symptoms

Risk Factors:
•Being female
•Older age (especially postmenopausal women)
•Prolonged vitamin D deficiency
•History of radiation therapy to the head or neck
•Lithium use
•Genetic conditions such as Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN)
•Family history of hyperparathyroidism

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take all prescribed medications as directed.
•Maintain adequate hydration unless restricted by the healthcare provider.
•Engage in regular weight-bearing exercise as tolerated to support bone health.
•Follow dietary recommendations regarding calcium and vitamin D intake.
•Monitor bone density as recommended.
•Complete laboratory testing for calcium, PTH, and kidney function as ordered.
•Report new or worsening bone pain, kidney stones, muscle weakness, or mood changes.
•Keep all scheduled endocrinology and PCP appointments.
•Discuss surgical options (parathyroidectomy) with the healthcare provider if recommended.

Hypothyroidism.education:
What is Hypothyroidism?
Hypothyroidism is a condition in which the thyroid gland, a butterfly-shaped gland located in the front of the neck, does not produce enough thyroid hormone. Thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) regulate the body's metabolism — the rate at which the body uses energy — and play a critical role in virtually every organ system, including the heart, brain, muscles, and digestive system. When thyroid hormone levels are too low, body processes slow down, affecting energy levels, weight, body temperature, heart rate, and mental function. The most common cause of hypothyroidism is Hashimoto's thyroiditis, an autoimmune condition in which the immune system gradually destroys thyroid tissue. Other causes include thyroid surgery, radiation therapy, certain medications (lithium, amiodarone), iodine deficiency, and pituitary gland disorders. Hypothyroidism develops gradually and symptoms may be subtle at first, often attributed to aging or stress. Left untreated, it can lead to elevated cholesterol, heart disease, depression, peripheral neuropathy, and in severe cases, myxedema coma — a life-threatening condition requiring emergency treatment. Treatment with synthetic thyroid hormone replacement (levothyroxine) is highly effective but must be taken consistently, on an empty stomach, and with careful attention to factors that affect absorption.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Fatigue or lack of energy
•Weight gain or difficulty losing weight
•Increased sensitivity to cold
•Constipation
•Dry skin and hair
•Hair loss or thinning
•Puffy face or swelling
•Hoarse voice
•Muscle weakness, aches, or stiffness
•Joint pain or stiffness
•Elevated cholesterol levels
•Slow heart rate
•Depression or mood changes
•Memory problems or difficulty concentrating
•Irregular or heavy menstrual periods

Risk Factors:
•Being female
•Age over 60
•Family history of thyroid disease
•Autoimmune disease (especially Hashimoto's thyroiditis)
•Previous thyroid surgery or radiation therapy
•Certain medications (lithium, amiodarone)
•Iodine deficiency or excess
•Pregnancy or postpartum period

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take thyroid hormone replacement medication (levothyroxine) exactly as prescribed.
•Take the medication on an empty stomach, at the same time each day, typically 30-60 minutes before breakfast.
•Do not stop or change the dose without consulting the healthcare provider.
•Avoid taking thyroid medication with calcium, iron supplements, or antacids, as they can interfere with absorption.
•Complete thyroid function laboratory tests (TSH) as ordered.
•Report new or worsening symptoms to the healthcare provider.
•Keep all scheduled endocrinology and PCP appointments.
•Maintain a balanced diet and regular physical activity as tolerated.

CKD.education:
What is Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)?
Chronic kidney disease is a progressive condition in which the kidneys gradually lose their ability to filter waste, excess fluids, and electrolytes from the blood. The kidneys perform many vital functions, including filtering about 200 quarts of blood daily, removing toxins and excess water through urine, regulating blood pressure, producing hormones that stimulate red blood cell production (erythropoietin), activating vitamin D for bone health, and maintaining the balance of minerals such as sodium, potassium, calcium, and phosphorus. When the kidneys are damaged, these functions decline, allowing waste products and fluid to accumulate in the body. CKD is classified into five stages based on the glomerular filtration rate (GFR), a measure of how well the kidneys are filtering. Stage 1 represents mild damage with normal function, while stage 5 (end-stage kidney disease) means the kidneys have lost nearly all function and dialysis or transplantation is needed. The two most common causes of CKD are diabetes and high blood pressure, which together account for the majority of cases. Early CKD often produces no symptoms, making regular screening through blood and urine tests critical for early detection. Treatment focuses on slowing progression by aggressively managing blood pressure, blood sugar, and other risk factors, following dietary restrictions for sodium, potassium, phosphorus, and protein as directed, avoiding nephrotoxic medications, and planning for dialysis or transplantation when appropriate.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Fatigue or weakness
•Swelling of the feet, ankles, legs, or face
•Changes in urination (more or less frequent, foamy, dark, or blood-tinged)
•Nausea, vomiting, or loss of appetite
•Persistent itching
•Muscle cramps, especially at night
•Shortness of breath
•Difficulty concentrating
•Trouble sleeping
•High blood pressure that is difficult to control
•Early CKD often has no symptoms

Risk Factors:
•Diabetes
•High blood pressure
•Heart disease
•Family history of kidney disease
•Obesity
•Older age
•Smoking
•Frequent use of NSAIDs or certain medications
•History of acute kidney injury
•African American, Hispanic, Native American, or Asian descent

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take all prescribed medications as directed, including blood pressure and diabetes medications.
•Follow dietary restrictions for sodium, potassium, phosphorus, and protein as directed.
•Maintain blood pressure and blood sugar within the provider-recommended range.
•Stay physically active as tolerated.
•Avoid NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) unless approved by the healthcare provider.
•Do not take supplements or herbal remedies without consulting the provider.
•Complete all recommended laboratory tests and imaging.
•Keep all scheduled nephrology and PCP appointments.
•Discuss dialysis planning or transplant evaluation if CKD progresses.
•Stop smoking.

BPH.education:
What is Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH)?
Benign prostatic hyperplasia is a common, non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate gland that occurs in most men as they age. The prostate gland surrounds the urethra (the tube that carries urine from the bladder out of the body). As the prostate grows larger, it can squeeze or partially obstruct the urethra, restricting the flow of urine and causing bothersome lower urinary tract symptoms. BPH is extremely common — approximately half of men between ages 51 and 60 and up to 90% of men over age 80 have some degree of prostate enlargement. BPH is not prostate cancer and does not increase the risk of developing prostate cancer. However, both conditions can coexist, which is why regular prostate health screening is important. The severity of symptoms does not always correlate directly with the size of the prostate — some men with significant enlargement have few symptoms, while others with minimal enlargement experience significant urinary difficulty. If left untreated, BPH can lead to complications including urinary tract infections, bladder stones, bladder damage, and acute urinary retention (a sudden inability to urinate, which requires emergency catheterization). Treatment options include lifestyle modifications, medications (alpha-blockers, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors), and minimally invasive or surgical procedures for more severe cases.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Frequent urination, especially at night (nocturia)
•Difficulty starting urination
•Weak or interrupted urine stream
•Feeling that the bladder is not completely empty
•Urgency to urinate
•Dribbling at the end of urination
•Straining to urinate
•Urinary retention (inability to urinate)

Risk Factors:
•Older age (especially over 50)
•Family history of BPH
•Obesity
•Diabetes and heart disease
•Sedentary lifestyle
•Certain ethnic backgrounds

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed medications as directed (alpha-blockers, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, or combination therapy).
•Report new or worsening urinary symptoms to the healthcare provider.
•Avoid medications that can worsen symptoms (decongestants, antihistamines) unless approved by the provider.
•Limit fluids in the evening to reduce nighttime urination.
•Avoid caffeine and alcohol, which can irritate the bladder.
•Urinate when the urge is first felt; do not delay.
•Practice double voiding (urinate, wait a moment, then try again).
•Stay physically active.
•Keep all scheduled urology and PCP appointments.

Urinary Incontinence.education:
What is Urinary Incontinence?
Urinary incontinence is the involuntary loss of urine — a condition that affects millions of people and ranges from occasionally leaking urine when coughing, sneezing, or laughing to having an urge to urinate that is so sudden and strong that reaching a toilet in time is difficult. While urinary incontinence is more common with aging, it is not an inevitable consequence of getting older. There are several types: stress incontinence (leaking during physical activity or pressure on the bladder), urge incontinence (sudden, intense urge followed by involuntary loss), overflow incontinence (frequent or constant dribbling due to incomplete bladder emptying), and functional incontinence (physical or cognitive limitations preventing timely access to a toilet). Many people experience mixed incontinence, combining features of more than one type. Urinary incontinence can significantly impact quality of life, leading to embarrassment, social isolation, anxiety, and skin problems. Effective treatments are available and depend on the type and severity, including behavioral therapies (bladder retraining, pelvic floor exercises), medications, medical devices, and surgical procedures. Proper incontinence care includes timely changing of incontinence products, thorough skin cleansing and drying, barrier cream application, and regular skin assessment to prevent breakdown and infection.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Leaking urine during physical activities (coughing, sneezing, laughing, exercising)
•Sudden, strong urge to urinate followed by involuntary loss of urine
•Frequent urination (more than 8 times in 24 hours)
•Nighttime urination
•Leaking urine without awareness
•Difficulty starting urination or weak urine stream
•Feeling that the bladder is not completely empty

Risk Factors:
•Older age
•Being female (pregnancy, childbirth, menopause)
•Prostate problems in men
•Obesity
•Neurological conditions
•Diabetes
•Chronic cough
•Pelvic surgery
•Urinary tract infections
•Certain medications

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Change incontinence products after each episode.
•Clean the skin gently after each episode.
•Pat the skin dry completely.
•Apply a barrier cream if recommended.
•Maintain adequate hydration unless restricted.
•Follow a regular toileting schedule.
•Wear clean, properly fitting absorbent products.
•Check the skin daily for redness, irritation, or breakdown.
•Wash hands before and after incontinence care.
•Practice pelvic floor exercises (Kegels) if recommended.
•Report fever, painful urination, blood in urine, worsening incontinence, or skin breakdown to the PCP promptly.
•Keep all scheduled urology, gynecology, and PCP appointments.

CVA/Stroke.education:
What is a Stroke (CVA)?
A stroke, or cerebrovascular accident, occurs when blood flow to a part of the brain is suddenly interrupted or when a blood vessel in the brain ruptures. Without oxygen-rich blood, brain cells begin to die within minutes, which can result in permanent brain damage, disability, or death. There are two main types: ischemic stroke, caused by a blood clot blocking an artery supplying the brain (accounting for about 87% of all strokes), and hemorrhagic stroke, caused by a blood vessel rupturing and bleeding into or around the brain. A transient ischemic attack (TIA), sometimes called a "mini-stroke," is a temporary blockage that resolves on its own but is a critical warning sign that a major stroke may follow. Stroke is a leading cause of serious long-term disability and the fifth leading cause of death in the United States. The effects of stroke depend on which area and how much of the brain is damaged, and can include paralysis or weakness on one side of the body, difficulty speaking or understanding speech, vision problems, memory loss, personality changes, and difficulty with daily activities. Recognizing stroke symptoms immediately and calling 911 is critical — treatments such as clot-dissolving medications (tPA) must be given within a narrow time window to be effective. After a stroke, rehabilitation therapies and aggressive risk factor management are essential to maximize recovery and prevent recurrence.

Signs and Symptoms (BE FAST):
•B – Balance: Sudden loss of balance or coordination
•E – Eyes: Sudden vision changes in one or both eyes
•F – Face: Facial drooping or uneven smile
•A – Arms: Arm weakness or numbness
•S – Speech: Slurred speech or difficulty speaking or understanding
•T – Time: Call 911 immediately if any symptoms occur
•Sudden severe headache with no known cause
•Sudden confusion
•Sudden numbness or weakness, especially on one side

•Atrial fibrillation
•Diabetes
•High cholesterol
•Smoking

•Excessive alcohol use
•Heart disease

•Family history of stroke
•Older age
•Sickle cell disease

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take all prescribed medications as directed, including blood thinners, blood pressure, cholesterol, and diabetes medications.
•Monitor blood pressure at home as directed.
•Participate in physical, occupational, and speech therapy as recommended.
•Follow a heart-healthy diet.
•Stay physically active as tolerated and approved by the provider.
•Stop smoking and avoid secondhand smoke.
•Limit alcohol intake.
•Know the BE FAST warning signs and teach them to family and caregivers.
•Attend all rehabilitation and follow-up appointments.
•Report new or recurring stroke symptoms immediately.

Heart-Healthy and Stroke Prevention Diet:
A heart-healthy diet reduces the risk of recurrent stroke by managing blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar. The DASH and Mediterranean diets are both recommended. Sodium restriction is important for blood pressure control. If swallowing difficulties (dysphagia) are present after stroke, follow the speech pathologist's recommendations for modified food textures and liquid consistencies.

Multiple Sclerosis.education:
What is Multiple Sclerosis (MS)?
Multiple sclerosis is a chronic autoimmune disease of the central nervous system in which the immune system mistakenly attacks myelin, the protective insulating sheath that surrounds nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord. When myelin is damaged (demyelination), it disrupts the electrical signals traveling along the nerves, causing communication problems between the brain and the rest of the body. Over time, the nerves themselves can deteriorate or become permanently damaged, leading to irreversible disability. MS is unpredictable — symptoms, severity, and progression vary widely from person to person. Some people experience mild symptoms and long periods of remission, while others have a more aggressive course with accumulating disability. The disease typically follows one of several patterns: relapsing-remitting MS (the most common form, with clearly defined relapses followed by recovery), secondary progressive MS, primary progressive MS, or progressive-relapsing MS. MS can affect virtually any neurological function, including vision, movement, sensation, coordination, bladder and bowel function, and cognition. While there is no cure, disease-modifying therapies can reduce the frequency and severity of relapses, slow disease progression, and reduce new areas of damage visible on MRI. Early treatment initiation is associated with better long-term outcomes.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Numbness, tingling, or weakness in one or more limbs
•Electric-shock sensations with certain neck movements
•Tremor or lack of coordination
•Unsteady gait or difficulty walking
•Vision problems (blurred vision, double vision, partial or complete vision loss)
•Fatigue
•Dizziness or vertigo
•Slurred speech
•Bladder and bowel dysfunction
•Cognitive changes (difficulty with memory, attention, problem-solving)
•Muscle stiffness or spasms
•Pain

Risk Factors:
•Being female (2-3 times more common in women)
•Age 20 to 50
•Family history of MS
•Northern European descent
•Living farther from the equator
•Low vitamin D levels
•Smoking
•Certain autoimmune diseases
•Certain viral infections (Epstein-Barr virus)

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take disease-modifying therapies and other medications exactly as prescribed.
•Do not stop or change medications without consulting the neurologist.
•Participate in physical and occupational therapy as recommended.
•Stay physically active with appropriate exercise as tolerated.
•Manage fatigue through energy conservation strategies.
•Avoid overheating, which can temporarily worsen symptoms.
•Report new or worsening symptoms (relapses) to the neurologist promptly.
•Maintain a balanced diet and healthy weight.
•Manage stress through healthy coping strategies.
•Keep all scheduled neurology and PCP appointments.
•Complete recommended laboratory monitoring for disease-modifying therapies.

Parkinson Disease.education:
What is Parkinson's Disease?
Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurological disorder that primarily affects movement but can also cause a wide range of non-motor symptoms. It occurs when nerve cells (neurons) in a part of the brain called the substantia nigra gradually break down or die. These neurons produce dopamine, a chemical messenger essential for smooth, coordinated movement. As dopamine levels decline, the brain loses its ability to properly control movement, leading to the characteristic symptoms of tremor, slowness, stiffness, and balance difficulties. Parkinson's disease affects approximately one million Americans and is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder after Alzheimer's disease. The cause of Parkinson's is not fully understood, but it is believed to involve a combination of genetic susceptibility and environmental factors. Symptoms typically begin on one side of the body and gradually affect both sides as the disease progresses. Beyond the well-known movement symptoms, Parkinson's can cause depression, anxiety, sleep disturbances, constipation, loss of smell, cognitive changes, autonomic dysfunction (blood pressure drops, urinary problems), and in later stages, dementia. While there is no cure, medications — particularly levodopa/carbidopa — can effectively manage symptoms, and physical therapy, exercise, and speech therapy play important roles in maintaining function and quality of life.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Tremors or shaking, commonly affecting the hands or arms
•Slowness of movement (bradykinesia)
•Muscle stiffness or rigidity
•Difficulty with balance or coordination
•Changes in walking, including small or shuffling steps
•Difficulty getting up from a chair or starting movement
•Changes in speech (softer, monotone) or facial expression
•Difficulty with handwriting or other fine motor activities
•Fatigue or sleep problems
•Constipation
•Depression, anxiety, or mood changes
•Memory or thinking changes
•Dizziness or lightheadedness, particularly when standing

Risk Factors:
•Older age (usually diagnosed after age 60)
•Male sex (slightly more common)
•Family history of Parkinson's disease
•Exposure to certain pesticides or herbicides
•Head trauma
•Certain genetic mutations

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take Parkinson's medications exactly as prescribed and at the scheduled times.
•Do not stop, skip, or change medications without consulting the healthcare provider.
•Use a pill organizer, written schedule, alarm, or phone reminder if needed.
•Keep an updated medication list and bring it to appointments.
•Report new or worsening symptoms or medication side effects to the neurologist.
•Notify the provider if medication appears to wear off sooner than expected.
•Remain physically active with walking, stretching, strengthening, and balance exercises.
•Participate in physical or occupational therapy when ordered.
•Change positions slowly, particularly when getting out of bed or standing.
•Use prescribed mobility or assistive devices consistently.
•Maintain regular appointments with the neurologist, PCP, and other specialists.

Seizure Disorders.education:
What are Seizure Disorders?
A seizure disorder, most commonly epilepsy, is a neurological condition characterized by recurrent, unprovoked seizures caused by abnormal, excessive electrical activity in the brain. Seizures can vary dramatically in type and severity — from brief lapses of attention or subtle muscle twitches (absence or myoclonic seizures) to full-body convulsions with loss of consciousness (tonic-clonic seizures). Epilepsy affects approximately 3.4 million Americans and can develop at any age, though it is most commonly diagnosed in children and older adults. A person is generally diagnosed with epilepsy after having two or more unprovoked seizures occurring more than 24 hours apart. Seizures can be caused by brain injury, stroke, brain tumors, infections (meningitis, encephalitis), genetic factors, developmental disorders, or abnormalities in brain structure, though in many cases the cause is unknown. Having uncontrolled seizures poses safety risks, including injury from falls, drowning, driving accidents, and in rare cases, sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP). Treatment with anti-seizure medications effectively controls seizures in about two-thirds of people with epilepsy. For those whose seizures do not respond to medications, options may include specialized diets (ketogenic diet), surgical treatment, vagus nerve stimulation, or responsive neurostimulation.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Uncontrollable jerking movements of the arms and legs
•Temporary confusion or staring spells
•Loss of consciousness or awareness
•Fear, anxiety, or a sense of deja vu before a seizure (aura)
•Stiffening of the body
•Falling suddenly
•Lip smacking, chewing, or other repetitive movements
•Temporary loss of bladder or bowel control
•Difficulty speaking during or after a seizure
•Fatigue, confusion, or headache after a seizure

Risk Factors:
•Family history of seizures or epilepsy
•Head trauma or traumatic brain injury
•Stroke or other cerebrovascular disease
•Brain infections (meningitis, encephalitis)
•Brain tumors
•Developmental disorders
•Prenatal injury or birth complications
•Alzheimer's disease or other neurodegenerative conditions
•High fever in childhood (febrile seizures)

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take anti-seizure medications exactly as prescribed, at the same times each day.
•Do not stop, skip, or change medications without consulting the neurologist.
•Keep a seizure diary recording date, time, duration, and description of each seizure.
•Get adequate sleep on a regular schedule.
•Avoid known seizure triggers (sleep deprivation, excessive alcohol, flashing lights, stress).
•Wear medical identification indicating seizure disorder.
•Follow driving restrictions as required by state law and the healthcare provider.
•Inform family, friends, and coworkers about seizure first aid.
•Keep all scheduled neurology and PCP appointments.
•Complete recommended blood work to monitor anti-seizure medication levels.
•Discuss safety precautions for swimming, bathing, heights, and operating machinery.

Spinal Cord Injury.education:
What is a Spinal Cord Injury (SCI)?
A spinal cord injury is damage to the spinal cord that results in temporary or permanent changes in strength, sensation, and body functions below the site of injury. The spinal cord, a bundle of nerves running through the vertebral column from the brain to the lower back, carries signals between the brain and the rest of the body. When the spinal cord is damaged, these signals are partially or completely disrupted. The severity of the injury depends on the location along the spinal cord and the extent of the damage. A complete injury means there is no voluntary movement or sensation below the level of injury; an incomplete injury means some function remains. Injuries higher on the spinal cord (cervical level) affect more of the body, potentially causing quadriplegia (impairment of all four limbs) and affecting breathing, while lower injuries (thoracic, lumbar) typically affect the legs and lower body (paraplegia). Spinal cord injuries create complex, lifelong medical needs including mobility challenges, bowel and bladder management, skin integrity maintenance, respiratory care, pain management, prevention of secondary complications (blood clots, pressure injuries, urinary tract infections, autonomic dysreflexia), and psychological adjustment. Rehabilitation is intensive and ongoing, involving physical therapy, occupational therapy, and adaptive equipment to maximize independence.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Loss of movement or paralysis below the level of injury
•Loss of sensation (touch, heat, cold) below the level of injury
•Loss of bowel or bladder control
•Spasms or exaggerated reflexes
•Pain or stinging sensations
•Difficulty breathing or coughing
•Changes in sexual function and fertility
•Autonomic dysreflexia (dangerously high blood pressure in injuries above T6)

Risk Factors:
•Motor vehicle accidents
•Falls
•Violence (gunshot or stab wounds)
•Sports and recreation injuries
•Older age (increased fall risk)
•Osteoporosis
•Spinal canal narrowing

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the rehabilitation plan and participate in physical and occupational therapy.
•Take all prescribed medications as directed.
•Perform regular skin checks to prevent pressure injuries.
•Follow bowel and bladder management programs as directed.
•Use prescribed mobility devices and adaptive equipment.
•Maintain respiratory hygiene if breathing is affected.
•Stay physically active as tolerated.
•Monitor for signs of autonomic dysreflexia (sudden severe headache, flushing, sweating above injury level).
•Prevent urinary tract infections through proper catheter care.
•Attend all rehabilitation, neurology, urology, and PCP appointments.
•Address mental health needs including depression and adjustment.

Christopher & Dana Reeve Foundation. (2024). Living with paralysis. https://www.christopherreeve.org

Traumatic Brain Injury.education:
What is Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI)?
A traumatic brain injury occurs when an external mechanical force causes damage to the brain. This can result from a violent blow, bump, or jolt to the head, the head striking an object, or a penetrating injury such as a gunshot wound. TBI severity ranges from mild (concussion) — the most common form — to severe, which can result in extended periods of unconsciousness, amnesia, and potentially permanent cognitive and physical disabilities. Even mild TBIs can cause persistent symptoms and should be taken seriously. Falls are the leading cause of TBI overall, while motor vehicle accidents are the leading cause of TBI-related hospitalization and death. The effects of TBI depend on the severity, location, and extent of the brain damage and can include headaches, cognitive impairment (memory, attention, executive function), behavioral and emotional changes (irritability, depression, anxiety, impulsivity), speech and language difficulties, sensory problems, motor deficits, sleep disturbances, and seizures. Recovery from TBI is highly variable — some people recover fully within weeks, while others experience permanent impairments. Post-concussion syndrome can cause symptoms lasting weeks to months after a mild TBI. Repeated TBIs are of particular concern because they can have cumulative effects, including chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). Rehabilitation may involve multiple specialties including neurology, neuropsychology, physical therapy, occupational therapy, and speech therapy.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Headache
•Confusion or disorientation
•Dizziness or loss of balance
•Nausea or vomiting
•Fatigue or drowsiness
•Difficulty speaking
•Memory problems or difficulty concentrating
•Mood changes, irritability, or depression
•Sleep disturbances
•Sensitivity to light or noise
•Blurred vision or ringing in the ears
•Seizures (in more severe cases)
•Loss of consciousness
•Weakness or numbness in extremities
•Persistent or worsening headache

Risk Factors:
•Falls (leading cause in older adults)
•Motor vehicle accidents
•Violence
•Sports and recreation injuries
•Military service and blast exposures
•Previous traumatic brain injury
•Older age or very young age
•Alcohol use

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the healthcare provider's instructions for rest and activity progression.
•Take all prescribed medications as directed.
•Gradually return to normal activities as approved by the healthcare provider.
•Get adequate sleep and rest.
•Avoid activities that risk another head injury until cleared.
•Use memory aids such as calendars, lists, and reminders.
•Participate in rehabilitation therapies (physical, occupational, speech, cognitive).
•Avoid alcohol and recreational drugs.
•Wear protective equipment during sports and activities.
•Report new or worsening symptoms to the healthcare provider.
•Attend all follow-up neurology and PCP appointments.
•Address emotional and mental health needs.

Alzheimer's.education:
What is Alzheimer's Disease?
Alzheimer's disease is a progressive, irreversible brain disorder that gradually destroys memory, thinking skills, and eventually the ability to carry out even the simplest daily tasks. It is the most common cause of dementia, accounting for 60-80% of all dementia cases. Alzheimer's disease involves the abnormal buildup of proteins in and around brain cells — amyloid plaques that accumulate between neurons and tau tangles that form inside neurons — which disrupts cell communication and ultimately leads to cell death and brain shrinkage. Symptoms typically develop slowly and worsen over time, progressing from mild forgetfulness to severe cognitive and functional impairment. In the early stages, a person may have trouble remembering recent events, conversations, or appointments. As the disease progresses, individuals may become confused about time and place, experience personality and behavioral changes, have difficulty speaking, swallowing, and walking, and eventually require full-time care. Alzheimer's is most commonly diagnosed in people over 65, and the risk increases significantly with age, though early-onset Alzheimer's can affect people in their 40s and 50s. There is currently no cure, but medications may temporarily slow symptom progression, and supportive care strategies, environmental modifications, and caregiver support are essential components of management.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Memory loss that disrupts daily life
•Difficulty planning or solving problems
•Difficulty completing familiar tasks
•Confusion with time or place
•Trouble understanding visual images and spatial relationships
•New problems with words in speaking or writing
•Misplacing things and losing the ability to retrace steps
•Decreased or poor judgment
•Withdrawal from work or social activities
•Changes in mood and personality
•Wandering or getting lost

Risk Factors:
•Older age (greatest risk factor)
•Family history of Alzheimer's
•Genetics (APOE-e4 gene)
•Down syndrome
•Head trauma
•Cardiovascular disease risk factors
•Social isolation
•Low education levels

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed medications as directed.
•Maintain a consistent daily routine.
•Use memory aids such as calendars, labeled photos, and written reminders.
•Keep the home safe by removing hazards and installing safety devices.
•Stay physically, mentally, and socially active as able.
•Ensure adequate nutrition and hydration.
•Attend all scheduled neurology, geriatrics, and PCP appointments.
•Plan for future care needs while the person can still participate in decisions.
•Seek caregiver support and respite care services.
•Address behavioral changes with the healthcare provider.

Anxiety.education:
What is an Anxiety Disorder?
Anxiety disorders are a group of mental health conditions characterized by excessive, persistent worry, fear, or nervousness that goes beyond normal everyday concerns and interferes with daily functioning. While occasional anxiety is a normal human emotion, anxiety disorders involve worry that is disproportionate to the situation, difficult to control, and persists over time. There are several types: generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) involves chronic, excessive worry about many areas of life; panic disorder involves recurrent, unexpected panic attacks — sudden episodes of intense fear with physical symptoms such as rapid heartbeat, sweating, trembling, and shortness of breath; social anxiety disorder involves intense fear of social situations and being judged; and specific phobias involve overwhelming fear of specific objects or situations. Anxiety disorders are the most common mental health conditions in the United States, affecting approximately 40 million adults. They are highly treatable, yet only about one-third of those affected receive treatment. Anxiety disorders are caused by a complex combination of genetic factors, brain chemistry, personality traits, and life experiences including trauma. Physical health conditions such as thyroid disorders, heart arrhythmias, and chronic pain can mimic or worsen anxiety symptoms. Effective treatments include cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), which is considered the gold standard, medications (SSRIs, SNRIs, buspirone), and lifestyle strategies including regular exercise, adequate sleep, stress management, and limiting caffeine and alcohol.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Excessive worry or fear that is difficult to control
•Feeling restless, wound-up, or on edge
•Being easily fatigued
•Difficulty concentrating or mind going blank
•Irritability
•Muscle tension
•Sleep problems (difficulty falling or staying asleep, restless sleep)
•Panic attacks (sudden periods of intense fear with physical symptoms)
•Rapid heartbeat or pounding heart
•Shortness of breath
•Sweating, trembling, or shaking
•Avoidance of situations that trigger anxiety

Risk Factors:
•Family history of anxiety or other mental health disorders
•Childhood trauma or adverse experiences
•Chronic medical conditions
•Substance use or withdrawal
•Significant life stress
•Personality traits (shyness, behavioral inhibition)
•Being female
•History of other mental health disorders

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed medications as directed (SSRIs, SNRIs, buspirone, or other medications).
•Attend therapy appointments (cognitive behavioral therapy is highly effective).
•Practice relaxation techniques such as deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, or meditation.
•Stay physically active with regular exercise.
•Maintain a regular sleep schedule.
•Limit caffeine and alcohol.
•Stay connected with family, friends, or support groups.
•Identify and manage personal anxiety triggers.
•Avoid self-medicating with alcohol or drugs.
•Keep all scheduled behavioral health and PCP appointments.

Bipolar Disorder.education:
What is Bipolar Disorder?
Bipolar disorder is a chronic mental health condition characterized by dramatic shifts in mood, energy, activity levels, concentration, and the ability to carry out daily tasks. These mood episodes are distinctly different from the normal ups and downs that everyone experiences. Manic episodes involve abnormally elevated mood, energy, and activity — a person may feel euphoric, unusually irritable, sleep very little yet feel fully rested, talk rapidly, have racing thoughts, and engage in impulsive or risky behaviors with potentially serious consequences (spending sprees, risky sexual behavior, poor business decisions). Depressive episodes involve persistent sadness, hopelessness, loss of interest in activities, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, changes in sleep and appetite, and in severe cases, thoughts of death or suicide. Some people experience mixed episodes with features of both mania and depression simultaneously. There are several types: Bipolar I involves full manic episodes, Bipolar II involves less severe hypomanic episodes with major depressive episodes, and cyclothymic disorder involves chronic fluctuating mood with periods of hypomania and mild depression. Bipolar disorder typically develops in late adolescence or early adulthood. It requires lifelong treatment, as stopping medication — even when feeling well — frequently triggers relapse. Treatment includes mood-stabilizing medications, atypical antipsychotics, and psychotherapy, with consistent medication adherence and routine maintenance being critical for stability.

Signs and Symptoms:
Manic Episode:
•Abnormally upbeat, jumpy, or wired
•Increased activity, energy, or agitation
•Exaggerated sense of well-being and self-confidence
•Decreased need for sleep
•Unusual talkativeness or rapid speech
•Racing thoughts
•Distractibility
•Poor decision-making (spending sprees, risky behavior)

Depressive Episode:
•Depressed mood, sadness, or hopelessness
•Loss of interest or pleasure in activities
•Significant weight loss or gain
•Insomnia or sleeping too much
•Fatigue or loss of energy
•Feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt
•Difficulty thinking, concentrating, or making decisions
•Thoughts of death or suicide

Risk Factors:
•Family history of bipolar disorder
•Periods of high stress or trauma
•Drug or alcohol use
•Major life changes

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take mood-stabilizing and other psychiatric medications exactly as prescribed.
•Do not stop or change medications without consulting the psychiatrist, even when feeling well.
•Attend all therapy and psychiatric appointments.
•Maintain a regular daily routine including consistent sleep, meal, and activity times.
•Monitor mood changes and keep a mood diary.
•Avoid alcohol and recreational drugs.
•Identify early warning signs of manic and depressive episodes.
•Build a support network of family, friends, and support groups.
•Develop a crisis plan with the healthcare provider.
•Stay physically active.
