Dementia.education:
What is Dementia?
Dementia is not a single disease but rather an umbrella term describing a group of symptoms associated with a decline in memory, reasoning, and other cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life. Dementia occurs when brain cells are damaged and can no longer communicate effectively with each other. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause, but other types include vascular dementia (caused by reduced blood flow to the brain, often after strokes), Lewy body dementia (caused by abnormal protein deposits called Lewy bodies), frontotemporal dementia (caused by degeneration of the frontal and temporal lobes), and mixed dementia (a combination of types). The specific symptoms experienced depend on which part of the brain is affected. Common features across all types include progressive memory loss, difficulty with language and communication, impaired judgment and reasoning, confusion about time and place, difficulty performing familiar tasks, personality and behavioral changes, and eventual loss of ability to perform self-care. Dementia is not a normal part of aging, though the risk increases significantly with age. While most forms of dementia are progressive and cannot be cured, early diagnosis allows for treatment planning, access to medications that may temporarily slow progression, implementation of safety measures, caregiver education and support, advance care planning, and connection with community resources.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Memory loss, especially short-term memory
•Difficulty with communication and finding words
•Difficulty with complex tasks and problem-solving
•Difficulty with planning and organizing
•Confusion and disorientation
•Personality and behavior changes
•Depression and anxiety
•Inappropriate behavior
•Paranoia or suspiciousness
•Agitation
•Hallucinations (in some types)
•Difficulty with coordination and motor functions (in some types)
•Wandering

Risk Factors:
•Older age
•Family history of dementia
•Cardiovascular disease and risk factors
•Diabetes
•Smoking
•Excessive alcohol use
•Depression
•Social isolation
•Head trauma
•Down syndrome
•Low education and cognitive engagement

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed medications as directed.
•Maintain a consistent daily routine.
•Keep the environment safe and familiar.
•Use memory aids and labels.
•Stay physically, mentally, and socially active as able.
•Ensure adequate nutrition and hydration.
•Manage behavioral symptoms with non-drug approaches first.
•Plan for future care needs while the person can participate.
•Attend all scheduled appointments.
•Seek caregiver support and respite care.
•Address legal and financial planning early.

Depression.education:
What is Depression?
Depression (major depressive disorder) is a common, serious, and treatable medical illness that negatively affects how a person feels, thinks, and handles daily activities. It is far more than "feeling sad" or going through a difficult time — depression involves persistent changes in brain chemistry and function that cause a constellation of emotional, cognitive, and physical symptoms lasting at least two weeks. Depression can make even basic activities like getting out of bed, eating, and bathing feel overwhelming. It affects approximately 21 million adults in the United States and is one of the leading causes of disability worldwide. Depression can occur at any age but often begins in adulthood, and it is more common in women than men. The causes are complex and multifactorial, involving genetic predisposition, brain chemistry imbalances (particularly serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine), hormonal changes, medical conditions (thyroid disease, chronic pain, heart disease), stressful life events, trauma, and substance use. Depression frequently co-occurs with anxiety, substance use disorders, and chronic medical conditions, making comprehensive assessment and treatment important. Depression is not a character weakness or something a person can simply "snap out of." Effective treatments include antidepressant medications, psychotherapy (particularly cognitive behavioral therapy and interpersonal therapy), or a combination of both, along with lifestyle modifications including regular exercise, adequate sleep, social connection, and stress management.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Persistent sad, anxious, or empty mood
•Feelings of hopelessness or pessimism
•Irritability
•Feelings of guilt, worthlessness, or helplessness
•Loss of interest or pleasure in hobbies and activities
•Decreased energy or fatigue
•Difficulty concentrating, remembering, or making decisions
•Difficulty sleeping, early-morning awakening, or oversleeping
•Appetite and/or weight changes
•Thoughts of death or suicide
•Aches, pains, headaches, or digestive problems without a clear physical cause
•Restlessness

Risk Factors:
•Family history of depression
•Personal history of depression or other mental health disorders
•Major life changes, trauma, or stress
•Chronic medical conditions
•Certain medications
•Substance use
•Social isolation
•Being female

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take antidepressant medications as prescribed.
•Do not stop or change medications without consulting the healthcare provider.
•Attend therapy or counseling appointments.
•Stay physically active with regular exercise.
•Maintain a regular sleep schedule.
•Stay connected with family, friends, or support groups.
•Practice stress-reduction techniques.
•Set small, achievable goals.
•Avoid alcohol and recreational drugs.
•Report worsening symptoms or thoughts of suicide to the healthcare provider immediately.
•Keep all scheduled behavioral health and PCP appointments.

PTSD.education:
What is Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)?
PTSD is a mental health condition that can develop after experiencing or witnessing a traumatic, life-threatening, or deeply distressing event such as military combat, sexual assault, physical violence, serious accidents, natural disasters, terrorism, or the sudden unexpected death of a loved one. While it is normal to experience fear, anxiety, and distress during and after a traumatic event, most people recover naturally over time. PTSD develops when the stress reaction persists and intensifies, disrupting the person's ability to function in daily life. PTSD affects approximately 6% of the U.S. population at some point in their lives, with women being twice as likely as men to develop the condition. The hallmark features of PTSD include intrusive re-experiencing of the trauma (flashbacks, nightmares, intrusive memories), persistent avoidance of reminders of the trauma, negative changes in thoughts and mood (emotional numbness, guilt, detachment from others, loss of interest in activities), and hyperarousal (being easily startled, hypervigilant, difficulty sleeping, irritability, difficulty concentrating). These symptoms can develop immediately after the trauma or may not appear until months or even years later. PTSD often co-occurs with depression, anxiety, substance use disorders, and chronic pain. Evidence-based treatments include trauma-focused psychotherapies (cognitive processing therapy, prolonged exposure therapy, EMDR) and medications (SSRIs, SNRIs), which can significantly reduce symptoms and improve quality of life.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Intrusive memories, flashbacks, or nightmares about the traumatic event
•Avoidance of people, places, activities, or situations that are reminders of the trauma
•Negative changes in thinking and mood (feeling hopeless, detached, emotionally numb)
•Loss of interest in activities previously enjoyed
•Feeling detached or estranged from others
•Difficulty experiencing positive emotions
•Being easily startled or frightened
•Hypervigilance (always being on guard)
•Trouble sleeping
•Difficulty concentrating
•Irritability, anger, or aggressive behavior
•Self-destructive behavior

Risk Factors:
•Exposure to traumatic events
•Prior trauma, especially childhood trauma
•Family or personal history of mental health disorders
•Lack of social support
•Ongoing stress after the event
•History of substance use
•Certain occupations (military, first responders, healthcare workers)

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed medications as directed.
•Attend therapy appointments (trauma-focused CBT, EMDR, or prolonged exposure therapy).
•Practice coping skills learned in therapy.
•Stay connected with supportive family, friends, or support groups.
•Stay physically active.
•Maintain a regular sleep schedule.
•Avoid alcohol and drug use.
•Learn and practice grounding techniques.
•Identify triggers and develop a plan for managing them.
•Keep all scheduled behavioral health and PCP appointments.

Schizophrenia.education:
What is Schizophrenia?
Schizophrenia is a chronic, severe mental health disorder that affects how a person thinks, feels, perceives reality, and behaves. It is characterized by episodes of psychosis — a disconnection from reality — along with cognitive difficulties and impaired social and occupational functioning. Schizophrenia affects approximately 1% of the world's population and typically manifests in late adolescence to early adulthood, though it can develop at any age. The disorder involves disruptions in brain chemistry and structure, particularly in dopamine and glutamate neurotransmitter systems. Symptoms are categorized into three groups: positive symptoms (features added to the person's experience, including hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking and speech), negative symptoms (features diminished or absent, including flat affect, reduced motivation, social withdrawal, and difficulty experiencing pleasure), and cognitive symptoms (impaired attention, concentration, working memory, and executive function). Schizophrenia is often misunderstood — it does not mean "split personality" and most people with schizophrenia are not violent. With consistent treatment, many people with schizophrenia can manage their symptoms and lead fulfilling lives. Treatment requires a combination of antipsychotic medications (which must be taken consistently, even when the person feels better), psychosocial therapies, supported employment and education, and strong social support systems.

Signs and Symptoms:
Positive symptoms:
•Hallucinations (hearing voices or seeing things that are not there)
•Delusions (false beliefs not based in reality)
•Thought disorders (unusual or dysfunctional ways of thinking)
•Movement disorders (agitated body movements)

Negative symptoms:
•Flat affect (reduced expression of emotions)
•Reduced feelings of pleasure in everyday life
•Difficulty beginning and sustaining activities
•Reduced speaking
•Social withdrawal

Cognitive symptoms:
•Poor executive functioning (difficulty understanding and using information)
•Difficulty focusing or paying attention
•Problems with working memory

Risk Factors:
•Family history of schizophrenia
•Brain chemistry and structure differences
•Prenatal exposure to viruses, malnutrition, or psychosocial factors
•Taking psychoactive drugs during adolescence
•Complications during birth

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take antipsychotic medications exactly as prescribed.
•Do not stop or change medications without consulting the psychiatrist, even when feeling better.
•Attend all therapy and psychiatric appointments.
•Participate in psychosocial treatments and rehabilitation.
•Maintain a consistent daily routine.
•Avoid alcohol and recreational drugs.
•Stay connected with supportive family, friends, or case managers.
•Report medication side effects to the healthcare provider.
•Develop a relapse prevention plan with the treatment team.
•Engage in meaningful activities and social connections as tolerated.

Substance-Related Disorders.education:
What are Substance-Related Disorders?
Substance-related disorders encompass substance use disorders (addiction) and substance-induced disorders caused by the problematic use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, illicit drugs, or other substances. Addiction is a chronic, relapsing brain disorder — not a moral failing or lack of willpower — characterized by compulsive substance seeking and use despite harmful consequences. Repeated substance exposure fundamentally changes the brain's reward, motivation, memory, and decision-making circuits, making it progressively harder for the person to control their use even when they want to stop. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) identifies 10 classes of substances that can lead to substance use disorders, including alcohol, opioids, stimulants, cannabis, sedatives, hallucinogens, and tobacco. Severity is classified as mild, moderate, or severe based on the number of diagnostic criteria met. Substance use disorders frequently co-occur with other mental health conditions — approximately half of people who experience a mental illness will also experience a substance use disorder at some point. Risk factors include genetics (accounting for 40-60% of vulnerability), early initiation of substance use, childhood trauma, mental health disorders, peer pressure, and environmental factors. Recovery is possible with appropriate treatment, which may include medication-assisted treatment (MAT), behavioral therapies, counseling, support groups, and addressing co-occurring mental and physical health conditions.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Strong urges or cravings to use the substance
•Inability to limit or control use
•Needing more of the substance to get the same effect (tolerance)
•Withdrawal symptoms when not using the substance
•Continuing use despite negative consequences
•Neglecting responsibilities at home, work, or school
•Social withdrawal or giving up activities
•Using the substance in dangerous situations
•Spending significant time obtaining, using, or recovering from the substance
•Failed attempts to stop or cut down use
•Changes in behavior, mood, or appearance

Risk Factors:
•Family history of addiction
•Mental health disorders (depression, anxiety, PTSD, ADHD)
•Peer pressure and social environment
•Early use of substances
•Childhood trauma or adverse experiences
•Chronic pain and opioid use
•Easy access to substances
•Lack of social support

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Participate in treatment programs (inpatient, outpatient, medication-assisted treatment).
•Take prescribed medications as directed (naltrexone, buprenorphine, methadone, or others).
•Attend therapy or counseling sessions.
•Participate in support groups (AA, NA, SMART Recovery).
•Develop a relapse prevention plan.
•Identify and avoid personal triggers.
•Build a sober support network.
•Stay physically active.
•Maintain a regular daily routine.
•Address co-occurring mental health conditions.
•Keep all scheduled treatment and PCP appointments.

Cirrhosis.education:
What is Cirrhosis?
Cirrhosis is the late stage of progressive liver scarring (fibrosis) caused by chronic liver disease. In cirrhosis, healthy liver tissue is replaced by scar tissue, which disrupts the liver's structure and impairs its ability to perform its many vital functions — including filtering toxins from the blood, producing bile for digestion, manufacturing proteins necessary for blood clotting, storing nutrients, and metabolizing medications. As more scar tissue forms, the liver gradually loses function, and blood flow through the liver is increasingly obstructed, leading to a dangerous rise in pressure within the portal vein system (portal hypertension). Portal hypertension can cause life-threatening complications including variceal bleeding (rupture of swollen veins in the esophagus or stomach), ascites (fluid accumulation in the abdomen), and hepatic encephalopathy (confusion and altered mental status caused by toxin buildup in the brain). Cirrhosis can result from many forms of chronic liver disease, with the most common causes being chronic hepatitis B or C infection, chronic alcohol use, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD/NASH). While cirrhosis cannot be reversed, treatment can slow or stop progression, manage complications, and improve quality of life. In advanced cases, liver transplantation may be necessary.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Fatigue and weakness
•Easy bruising or bleeding
•Yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice)
•Itchy skin
•Swelling in the abdomen (ascites)
•Swelling of the legs and ankles
•Nausea and loss of appetite
•Weight loss
•Spider-like blood vessels on the skin
•Confusion, drowsiness, or slurred speech (hepatic encephalopathy)
•Dark urine
•Pale-colored stools

Risk Factors:
•Chronic alcohol use
•Chronic hepatitis B or C infection
•Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD/NASH)
•Autoimmune hepatitis
•Bile duct diseases
•Certain genetic conditions
•Obesity and diabetes
•Certain medications or toxins

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take all prescribed medications as directed.
•Avoid all alcohol.
•Follow dietary restrictions for sodium and protein as directed.
•Take lactulose or rifaximin as prescribed for encephalopathy prevention.
•Weigh yourself daily and report sudden weight gain.
•Report new or worsening confusion, drowsiness, or personality changes.
•Complete recommended laboratory tests and imaging.
•Receive hepatitis A and B vaccinations if not already immune.
•Avoid NSAIDs and acetaminophen in excess.
•Discuss liver transplant evaluation with the provider if appropriate.
•Keep all scheduled hepatology and PCP appointments.

Crohn's Disease.education:
What is Crohn's Disease?
Crohn's disease is a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) that causes chronic inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract. Unlike ulcerative colitis, which only affects the colon, Crohn's disease can affect any part of the GI tract from the mouth to the anus, though it most commonly involves the end of the small intestine (ileum) and the beginning of the colon. The inflammation in Crohn's disease can extend through the entire thickness of the intestinal wall, and affected areas are often interspersed with healthy segments ("skip lesions"). This pattern of deep, transmural inflammation can lead to complications including strictures (narrowing of the intestine), fistulas (abnormal tunnels between the intestine and other structures), abscesses, and bowel obstruction. Crohn's disease is a chronic condition with periods of flare-ups and remission. The exact cause is unknown but involves a complex interplay of genetic susceptibility, immune system dysfunction, and environmental triggers. Cigarette smoking is the strongest controllable risk factor and worsens disease course. Treatment aims to reduce inflammation, achieve and maintain remission, prevent complications, and improve nutrition and quality of life through medications (aminosalicylates, corticosteroids, immunomodulators, biologics), dietary management, and when necessary, surgery.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Diarrhea (sometimes bloody)
•Abdominal pain and cramping
•Fatigue
•Unintended weight loss
•Fever
•Mouth sores
•Reduced appetite
•Perianal disease (pain, drainage, or fistulas near the anus)
•Joint pain
•Eye inflammation
•Skin rashes
•Delayed growth in children

Risk Factors:
•Family history of IBD
•Younger age (often diagnosed before age 30)
•Cigarette smoking (strongest controllable risk factor)
•Certain ethnic backgrounds (Ashkenazi Jewish descent)
•NSAIDs and certain medications may worsen the condition
•Living in urban or industrialized areas
•Diet high in processed foods

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed medications as directed (aminosalicylates, corticosteroids, immunomodulators, biologics).
•Do not stop medications without consulting the gastroenterologist.
•Follow dietary recommendations from the healthcare team.
•Stay hydrated.
•Stop smoking.
•Manage stress.
•Keep a food diary to identify trigger foods.
•Complete recommended laboratory tests and colonoscopies.
•Report flare symptoms promptly.
•Keep all scheduled gastroenterology and PCP appointments.

diet.diet_education:
IBD Nutrition — Flare vs. Remission:
Nutritional needs differ during active flares compared to periods of remission. During a flare, a low-residue or low-fiber diet with soft, easily digestible foods may help reduce symptoms. During remission, a well-balanced diet that gradually reintroduces fiber and a wider variety of foods is encouraged. Keeping a food diary helps identify individual trigger foods. Working with a dietitian experienced in inflammatory bowel disease is recommended.

During remission, a varied, nutrient-rich diet with gradual fiber reintroduction is recommended. Keeping a food diary helps identify personal trigger foods. Working with a dietitian experienced in IBD is highly recommended.

Inflammatory Bowel Disease.education:
What is Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)?
Inflammatory bowel disease is a term encompassing two chronic conditions — Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis — that involve persistent inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract. In ulcerative colitis, inflammation is limited to the innermost lining (mucosa) of the colon and rectum, typically starting at the rectum and extending in a continuous pattern. In Crohn's disease, inflammation can affect any part of the GI tract and extends through the full thickness of the bowel wall. Both conditions are characterized by periods of active disease (flares) alternating with periods of remission. IBD affects approximately 3 million adults in the United States, and the incidence is increasing worldwide. The exact cause is not fully understood but involves a dysregulated immune response in genetically susceptible individuals, triggered by environmental factors including alterations in the gut microbiome. IBD can significantly impact quality of life through persistent symptoms, nutritional deficiencies, fatigue, the need for frequent medical appointments, and the psychosocial burden of living with a chronic illness. Long-standing IBD also increases the risk of colorectal cancer, making regular surveillance colonoscopies important. Treatment is tailored to disease type, location, severity, and response, using a step-up approach from aminosalicylates to corticosteroids, immunomodulators, and biologic therapies.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Persistent diarrhea
•Abdominal pain and cramping
•Rectal bleeding or bloody stools
•Urgency to have a bowel movement
•Fatigue
•Unintended weight loss
•Reduced appetite
•Fever during flares
•Joint pain
•Skin problems
•Eye inflammation

Risk Factors:
•Family history of IBD
•Age (most often diagnosed in teens and young adults)
•Certain ethnic backgrounds
•Cigarette smoking (increases risk for Crohn's)
•Environmental factors
•Prior use of NSAIDs or antibiotics

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed medications as directed.
•Follow dietary recommendations.
•Stay hydrated, especially during flares.
•Stop smoking.
•Manage stress.
•Complete recommended colonoscopies and laboratory tests.
•Report flare symptoms promptly.
•Keep all scheduled gastroenterology appointments.
•Discuss colorectal cancer screening as IBD increases this risk.

IBD Nutrition — Flare vs. Remission:
Nutritional management of IBD varies depending on whether the disease is active (flare) or in remission. During flares, a low-fiber, bland diet with small frequent meals may be better tolerated. Nutritional deficiencies are common and may require supplementation.

Individual tolerance varies, and a food diary can help identify trigger foods.

Liver Disease.education:
What is Liver Disease?
Liver disease is a broad term encompassing any condition that damages the liver and impairs its function. The liver is one of the body's largest and most vital organs, performing over 500 essential functions including filtering blood and removing toxins, producing bile for fat digestion, manufacturing proteins for blood clotting and immune function, storing nutrients (vitamins, minerals, glycogen), metabolizing medications and hormones, and regulating cholesterol and blood sugar. Because the liver has a remarkable ability to regenerate, liver disease can progress silently for years before symptoms appear. When damage accumulates faster than the liver can repair itself, scarring (fibrosis) develops, which can eventually progress to cirrhosis — the advanced stage of liver disease where function is severely impaired. Major categories of liver disease include viral hepatitis (hepatitis A, B, C), alcohol-related liver disease, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), autoimmune hepatitis, genetic conditions (hemochromatosis, Wilson's disease), bile duct disorders, and liver cancer. Early detection through liver function blood tests is important because many forms of liver disease are treatable or manageable if caught before cirrhosis develops. Treatment depends on the specific type and may include antiviral medications, alcohol cessation, weight loss, immunosuppressive therapy, and in advanced cases, liver transplantation.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice)
•Abdominal pain and swelling
•Swelling of the legs and ankles
•Itchy skin
•Dark urine
•Pale or bloody stools
•Chronic fatigue
•Nausea or vomiting
•Loss of appetite
•Easy bruising
•Confusion or difficulty thinking (in advanced disease)

Risk Factors:
•Heavy alcohol use
•Obesity
•Type 2 diabetes
•Hepatitis B or C infection
•Exposure to toxins or certain chemicals
•Certain medications
•Family history of liver disease
•Autoimmune conditions

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed medications as directed.
•Avoid all alcohol.
•Maintain a healthy weight.
•Follow dietary recommendations.
•Avoid medications that can harm the liver (consult provider before taking any OTC medications).
•Get vaccinated for hepatitis A and B if not already immune.
•Complete recommended laboratory tests.
•Keep all scheduled hepatology and PCP appointments.
•Report new or worsening symptoms promptly.

NASH.education:
What is NASH (Non-Alcoholic Steatohepatitis)?
NASH is a progressive form of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) characterized by not only excess fat accumulation in the liver but also active inflammation and liver cell damage (hepatocyte injury). While simple fatty liver (steatosis) is generally benign and does not cause significant liver damage, NASH represents a more aggressive disease process that can lead to progressive fibrosis (scarring), cirrhosis, liver failure, and hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cancer). NASH is closely associated with metabolic syndrome — a cluster of conditions including obesity, type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance, high blood pressure, and abnormal cholesterol and triglyceride levels. It has become one of the most common causes of chronic liver disease worldwide and is rapidly becoming a leading indication for liver transplantation. NASH is estimated to affect 3-5% of the global population. The disease is often "silent," with many patients having no symptoms until significant liver damage has occurred. Diagnosis typically requires a combination of blood tests, imaging, and sometimes liver biopsy. The cornerstone of NASH treatment is lifestyle modification — specifically, gradual weight loss of 7-10% of body weight through a balanced diet (Mediterranean dietary pattern is preferred), regular exercise, and management of metabolic risk factors. Several pharmaceutical treatments are in development, and managing coexisting diabetes, cholesterol, and blood pressure is critical.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Most people with NASH have no symptoms in early stages
•Fatigue
•Pain or discomfort in the upper right abdomen
•Enlarged liver
•Jaundice (in advanced cases)
•Swelling of the abdomen or legs (in advanced cases)
•Spider-like blood vessels (in advanced cases)
•General malaise

Risk Factors:
•Overweight or obesity
•Type 2 diabetes or insulin resistance
•High cholesterol or triglycerides
•Metabolic syndrome
•Polycystic ovary syndrome
•Sleep apnea
•Hypothyroidism
•Older age
•Hispanic or Asian ethnicity

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Lose weight gradually if overweight (7-10% body weight loss can improve NASH).
•Follow a healthy, balanced diet.
•Exercise regularly as tolerated.
•Control blood sugar, cholesterol, and triglycerides.
•Avoid alcohol.
•Avoid unnecessary medications that may stress the liver.
•Take prescribed medications as directed.
•Complete recommended laboratory tests and imaging.
•Keep all scheduled hepatology and PCP appointments.

Arthritis.education:
What is Arthritis?
Arthritis is a broad term referring to more than 100 conditions that cause inflammation, pain, stiffness, and decreased range of motion in the joints. The two most common forms are osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease in which the protective cartilage that cushions the ends of bones gradually wears away, causing the bones to rub together. It most commonly affects the knees, hips, hands, and spine, and is associated with aging, joint injury, obesity, and repetitive stress. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the synovial membrane lining the joints, causing inflammation, swelling, and eventual destruction of cartilage and bone. RA can also affect other body systems including the skin, eyes, lungs, heart, and blood vessels. Arthritis is the leading cause of disability in the United States, affecting over 54 million adults. While there is no cure for most forms of arthritis, early and appropriate treatment can significantly reduce pain, prevent or slow joint damage, improve function, and maintain quality of life. Treatment approaches vary by type and may include anti-inflammatory and disease-modifying medications, physical therapy, joint protection strategies, weight management (excess weight places additional stress on weight-bearing joints), regular low-impact exercise, and in advanced cases, joint replacement surgery.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Joint pain
•Stiffness, especially in the morning or after inactivity
•Swelling of joints
•Redness and warmth around affected joints
•Decreased range of motion
•Fatigue
•Joint deformity (in advanced cases)
•Grinding or crunching sensation in the joints

Risk Factors:
•Older age
•Being female (rheumatoid arthritis)
•Family history of arthritis
•Previous joint injury
•Obesity (increases stress on weight-bearing joints)
•Smoking
•Certain occupations with repetitive joint stress

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take pain or arthritis medications as prescribed.
•Stay physically active with low-impact activities (walking, swimming, stretching).
•Protect joints and use proper body mechanics.
•Balance activity and rest.
•Maintain a healthy weight.
•Use heat or cold safely as recommended.
•Eat a balanced, anti-inflammatory diet.
•Prevent falls by keeping walking areas clear and wearing supportive footwear.
•Monitor symptoms and report persistent or worsening pain, swelling, or decreased mobility.
•Keep all scheduled PCP, rheumatology, or orthopedic appointments.

Back Pain.education:
What is Chronic Back Pain?
Chronic back pain is pain that persists for 12 weeks or longer, even after an initial injury or underlying cause has been treated. Back pain is one of the most common reasons for missed work and doctor visits, and it is a leading cause of disability worldwide. The back is a complex structure of bones (vertebrae), intervertebral discs (cushions between vertebrae), muscles, ligaments, tendons, and nerves, and problems with any of these components can cause pain. Chronic back pain can result from degenerative disc disease, spinal stenosis, herniated discs, osteoarthritis, compression fractures, muscle or ligament strain, scoliosis, or in some cases, no identifiable structural cause. Pain may be localized to the back or may radiate to the buttocks, legs, or feet (sciatica) when nerves are compressed or irritated. Chronic back pain often has both physical and psychological components — depression, anxiety, stress, and poor sleep can amplify pain perception and impair coping. A multidisciplinary approach to management is most effective and typically includes physical therapy to improve core strength, flexibility, and body mechanics; pain medications used judiciously; psychological strategies such as cognitive behavioral therapy; regular physical activity; weight management; ergonomic modifications; and avoidance of prolonged bed rest, which can actually worsen outcomes.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Persistent aching or stiffness along the spine
•Sharp, localized pain in the neck, upper back, or lower back
•Pain that radiates from the low back to the buttock, leg, or foot (sciatica)
•Inability to stand straight without pain
•Muscle spasms
•Decreased range of motion
•Numbness or tingling in the legs or feet
•Pain that worsens with certain activities, prolonged sitting, or standing

Risk Factors:
•Older age
•Lack of physical activity
•Overweight or obesity
•Improper lifting techniques
•Smoking
•Psychological conditions (depression, anxiety, stress)
•Occupational factors (heavy lifting, prolonged sitting)
•Previous back injuries
•Degenerative disc disease or spinal conditions

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed medications as directed.
•Stay physically active; avoid prolonged bed rest.
•Participate in physical therapy as recommended.
•Practice proper body mechanics and lifting techniques.
•Maintain a healthy weight.
•Use heat or cold therapy as recommended.
•Practice core-strengthening exercises.
•Maintain good posture.
•Use ergonomic furniture and support when sitting.
•Manage stress through relaxation techniques.
•Stop smoking.
•Keep all scheduled PCP, orthopedic, and physical therapy appointments.

DDD.education:
What is Degenerative Disc Disease (DDD)?
Degenerative disc disease is a condition in which the intervertebral discs — the tough, flexible cushions between the vertebrae of the spine — gradually break down as part of the aging process. Despite its name, DDD is not actually a disease but rather a normal degenerative process that occurs to some degree in virtually everyone as they age. The discs serve as shock absorbers for the spine, allowing flexibility and movement. Over time, the discs lose water content, making them less flexible and thinner, which reduces their ability to cushion the vertebrae. The disc's outer wall may develop small tears, and the gel-like center may bulge or herniate through weakened areas. These changes can lead to pain, instability, and in some cases, compression of nearby nerves. While virtually everyone's discs degenerate with age, not everyone experiences symptoms — the degree of pain and disability varies greatly among individuals. DDD most commonly affects the cervical (neck) and lumbar (lower back) regions of the spine. Treatment is typically conservative and focuses on pain management, maintaining mobility and function, and preventing further deterioration through physical therapy, core strengthening, proper posture and body mechanics, weight management, anti-inflammatory medications, and in some cases, epidural steroid injections or surgery for severe, refractory symptoms.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Pain in the neck, mid-back, or lower back
•Pain that may radiate to the arms, hands, buttocks, or legs
•Pain that worsens with sitting, bending, lifting, or twisting
•Pain that improves with walking, movement, or changing positions
•Numbness or tingling in the extremities
•Muscle weakness
•Stiffness in the spine
•Episodes of severe pain that gradually improve
•Decreased range of motion

Risk Factors:
•Aging (natural wear and tear)
•Repetitive physical activities
•Spinal injuries
•Obesity
•Smoking (reduces blood supply to discs)
•Genetics
•Occupations requiring heavy lifting or prolonged sitting

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed pain medications, anti-inflammatories, or muscle relaxants as directed.
•Participate in physical therapy to strengthen core and back muscles.
•Stay physically active with low-impact exercises.
•Maintain proper posture and body mechanics.
•Use heat or cold therapy as recommended.
•Maintain a healthy weight.
•Stop smoking.
•Use ergonomic supports when sitting or sleeping.
•Avoid activities that aggravate symptoms.
•Consider epidural steroid injections or surgical options if recommended.

Osteoporosis.education:
What is Osteoporosis?
Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disease characterized by low bone density and deterioration of bone tissue, resulting in fragile bones that are highly susceptible to fractures. Bone is living tissue that is constantly being broken down (resorption) and rebuilt (formation). Osteoporosis develops when the body loses too much bone, makes too little bone, or both, causing bones to become porous, weak, and brittle. In severe cases, even mild stress such as bending over, coughing, or a minor bump can cause a fracture. Osteoporosis-related fractures most commonly occur in the hip, spine (vertebral compression fractures), and wrist. Hip fractures are particularly devastating in older adults, often leading to loss of independence, nursing home placement, and increased mortality — about 20% of people who sustain a hip fracture die within one year. Osteoporosis is often called a "silent disease" because bone loss occurs without symptoms until a fracture happens. An estimated 10 million Americans have osteoporosis, and another 44 million have low bone density (osteopenia), placing them at increased risk. Risk factors include being female (especially postmenopausal), older age, small body frame, family history, low calcium and vitamin D intake, sedentary lifestyle, smoking, excessive alcohol use, and certain medications (long-term corticosteroids). Prevention and treatment focus on maximizing bone density through adequate calcium and vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, fall prevention, and when indicated, prescription medications that slow bone loss or stimulate bone formation.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Osteoporosis is often called a "silent disease" because there are usually no symptoms until a fracture occurs
•Back pain caused by a fractured or collapsed vertebra
•Loss of height over time
•Stooped posture (kyphosis)
•A bone that breaks more easily than expected

Risk Factors:
•Being female (especially postmenopausal)
•Older age
•Small body frame
•Family history of osteoporosis or fractures
•Low calcium or vitamin D intake
•Sedentary lifestyle
•Smoking
•Excessive alcohol consumption
•Certain medications (long-term corticosteroids, some seizure medications)
•Certain medical conditions (rheumatoid arthritis, hyperthyroidism, celiac disease)
•Early menopause
•Low estrogen or testosterone levels

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed osteoporosis medications as directed (bisphosphonates, denosumab, or others).
•Take calcium and vitamin D supplements as recommended by the healthcare provider.
•Engage in regular weight-bearing and muscle-strengthening exercises.
•Prevent falls by removing home hazards, using handrails, wearing supportive shoes, and improving lighting.
•Avoid smoking.
•Limit alcohol intake.
•Complete bone density testing (DEXA scan) as recommended.
•Use proper body mechanics when lifting.
•Keep all scheduled PCP, endocrinology, or rheumatology appointments.

Anemia.education:
What is Anemia?
Anemia is a condition in which the blood lacks enough healthy red blood cells or hemoglobin to carry adequate oxygen to the body's tissues. Hemoglobin is the iron-rich protein in red blood cells that binds to oxygen in the lungs and delivers it to organs and tissues throughout the body. When the body does not receive enough oxygen, it cannot function optimally, leading to symptoms such as fatigue, weakness, shortness of breath, and dizziness. Anemia is the most common blood disorder worldwide, affecting approximately 3 million Americans. There are many types of anemia with different causes: iron deficiency anemia (the most common form, caused by insufficient iron to produce hemoglobin), vitamin deficiency anemia (lack of B12 or folate), anemia of chronic disease (associated with chronic conditions like CKD, cancer, or autoimmune diseases), aplastic anemia (bone marrow failure), hemolytic anemia (premature destruction of red blood cells), and inherited forms such as sickle cell disease and thalassemia. Iron deficiency anemia can result from inadequate dietary iron intake, poor iron absorption (celiac disease, gastric bypass), chronic blood loss (heavy menstruation, GI bleeding from ulcers, polyps, or cancer), or increased iron demands (pregnancy). Treatment depends on the type and cause — iron deficiency anemia is treated with iron supplementation and addressing the underlying cause of blood loss, while other types may require B12 injections, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, blood transfusions, or treatment of the underlying disease.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Fatigue and weakness
•Pale or yellowish skin
•Shortness of breath
•Dizziness or lightheadedness
•Cold hands and feet
•Rapid or irregular heartbeat
•Headache
•Chest pain
•Brittle nails
•Unusual cravings for non-food items (pica)
•Difficulty concentrating
•Leg cramps

Risk Factors:
•Diet lacking in iron, vitamin B12, folate, or vitamin C
•Chronic conditions (CKD, cancer, inflammatory diseases)
•Heavy menstrual periods
•Pregnancy
•GI conditions causing blood loss or malabsorption
•Family history (sickle cell, thalassemia)
•Older age
•Chronic infections
•Autoimmune disorders

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed iron, vitamin B12, folate, or other supplements as directed.
•Take iron supplements on an empty stomach with vitamin C to improve absorption (unless GI upset occurs).
•Avoid taking iron supplements with calcium, dairy, coffee, or tea.
•Eat iron-rich and nutrient-dense foods.
•Complete recommended laboratory tests to monitor hemoglobin and iron levels.
•Report worsening fatigue, shortness of breath, or chest pain.
•Address underlying causes with the healthcare provider.

Sickle Cell Disease.education:
What is Sickle Cell Disease?
Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a group of inherited red blood cell disorders caused by a mutation in the gene that produces hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. In SCD, the body produces an abnormal form of hemoglobin called hemoglobin S. When hemoglobin S molecules release oxygen, they can polymerize and cause the normally round, flexible red blood cells to become rigid, sticky, and shaped like crescent moons or sickles. These misshapen cells cannot flow smoothly through small blood vessels and can clump together and stick to vessel walls, blocking blood flow and causing episodes of severe pain (vaso-occlusive crises), organ damage, and potentially life-threatening complications. SCD is an autosomal recessive condition, meaning a person must inherit two copies of the sickle cell gene (one from each parent) to have the disease. Having one copy makes a person a carrier (sickle cell trait), which usually causes no symptoms. SCD predominantly affects people of African descent but also occurs in Hispanic, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and South Asian populations. Complications include acute chest syndrome (a leading cause of death in SCD), stroke, splenic sequestration, chronic organ damage (kidneys, eyes, lungs, liver), chronic pain, leg ulcers, and increased susceptibility to infections. Treatment includes hydroxyurea (which increases fetal hemoglobin production and reduces sickling), pain management, blood transfusions, infection prevention, and in some cases, bone marrow/stem cell transplantation, which is the only current cure.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Episodes of severe pain (pain crises) in the chest, abdomen, joints, or bones
•Chronic pain
•Fatigue and anemia
•Swelling of the hands and feet (especially in young children)
•Frequent infections
•Delayed growth
•Vision problems
•Jaundice (yellowing of skin and eyes)
•Shortness of breath
•Stroke symptoms
•Priapism (painful, prolonged erections)

Risk Factors:
•Inherited condition requiring sickle cell gene from both parents
•African American descent (most common in the US)
•Hispanic, Middle Eastern, South Asian, and Mediterranean descent

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed medications as directed, including hydroxyurea and pain medications.
•Stay well-hydrated.
•Avoid extreme temperatures.
•Avoid high altitudes and unpressurized aircraft.
•Get regular exercise but avoid overexertion.
•Receive recommended vaccinations, including pneumococcal, meningococcal, influenza, and COVID-19.
•Take prescribed penicillin prophylaxis if directed.
•Complete regular health screenings (eyes, kidneys, lungs).
•Know the signs of stroke and splenic sequestration.
•Have a pain management plan for crises.
•Keep all scheduled hematology and PCP appointments.

Hearing Issues.education:
What are Hearing Issues?
Hearing loss is a partial or total inability to hear sounds in one or both ears, ranging from mild difficulty hearing soft sounds to profound deafness. It is the third most common chronic physical condition in the United States, affecting approximately 48 million Americans. Hearing loss can be classified by type: conductive (caused by problems in the outer or middle ear that block sound transmission), sensorineural (caused by damage to the inner ear or auditory nerve, which is the most common type), or mixed (a combination of both). The most common causes are age-related hearing loss (presbycusis), which affects one-third of adults over 65, and noise-induced hearing loss from chronic exposure to loud sounds. Other causes include ear infections, head trauma, certain medications (ototoxic drugs including some antibiotics, chemotherapy agents, and high-dose aspirin), genetic factors, and diseases such as Meniere's disease and otosclerosis. Untreated hearing loss has far-reaching consequences beyond communication difficulty — it is associated with social isolation, depression, cognitive decline, increased risk of dementia, decreased quality of life, and safety hazards. Modern hearing aids are sophisticated digital devices that can be customized to an individual's specific hearing loss pattern, and cochlear implants may be an option for severe to profound hearing loss. Early identification and intervention significantly improve outcomes.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Difficulty hearing conversations, especially in noisy environments
•Frequently asking others to repeat themselves
•Turning up the volume on TV, radio, or phone
•Difficulty hearing on the telephone
•Muffled hearing
•Ringing, buzzing, or hissing in the ears (tinnitus)
•Difficulty understanding speech, especially high-pitched voices
•Withdrawal from social situations due to difficulty hearing
•Feeling that others are mumbling

Risk Factors:
•Aging (presbycusis)
•Chronic exposure to loud noises
•Family history of hearing loss
•Certain medications (ototoxic drugs)
•Chronic ear infections
•Head trauma
•Diabetes and cardiovascular disease
•Smoking

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Use prescribed hearing aids consistently and maintain them properly.
•Attend regular audiology appointments for hearing evaluations and hearing aid adjustments.
•Protect hearing by avoiding loud noise exposure and using ear protection.
•Face the speaker and maintain eye contact during conversations.
•Reduce background noise when possible.
•Use assistive listening devices, captioning, or visual alerts as needed.
•Keep ears clean but avoid inserting objects into the ear canal.
•Report sudden hearing loss, ear pain, or drainage immediately.
•Keep all scheduled audiology and ENT appointments.

Cancer.education:
What is Cancer?
Cancer is a broad term for a group of diseases characterized by the uncontrolled growth and spread of abnormal cells. Normally, the body's cells grow, divide, and die in an orderly process. Cancer develops when genetic mutations cause cells to ignore the normal signals that control growth, allowing them to multiply uncontrollably and potentially invade surrounding tissues or spread to distant parts of the body through the blood and lymphatic systems (metastasis). There are more than 100 different types of cancer, each classified by the type of cell or organ in which it originates. Cancer is the second leading cause of death in the United States, after heart disease. However, survival rates have improved significantly due to advances in screening, early detection, and treatment. Risk factors vary by cancer type but broadly include tobacco use (the single largest preventable cause of cancer), excessive alcohol consumption, obesity, physical inactivity, poor diet, excessive UV exposure, certain infections (HPV, hepatitis B and C), exposure to environmental carcinogens, chronic inflammation, immunosuppression, genetics and family history, and older age. Treatment depends on the type, stage, and location of the cancer and may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, hormone therapy, stem cell transplantation, or a combination. Supportive and palliative care addresses symptom management, quality of life, and emotional well-being throughout the cancer journey.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Unexplained weight loss
•Fatigue that does not improve with rest
•Pain that does not go away
•Skin changes (darkening, yellowing, redness, sores that do not heal)
•Changes in bowel or bladder habits
•Persistent cough or trouble breathing
•Difficulty swallowing
•Unusual bleeding or discharge
•Lumps or thickening in the body
•Fever or night sweats
•Changes in moles or skin spots

Risk Factors:
•Older age
•Family history of cancer
•Tobacco use
•Excessive alcohol consumption
•Obesity
•Excessive sun exposure
•Exposure to radiation or certain chemicals
•Certain infections (HPV, hepatitis)
•Chronic inflammation
•Immunosuppression
•Sedentary lifestyle
•Poor diet

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the treatment plan prescribed by the oncology team.
•Take all prescribed medications as directed.
•Attend all scheduled chemotherapy, radiation, or immunotherapy sessions.
•Report side effects from treatment to the oncology team.
•Maintain adequate nutrition and hydration.
•Stay physically active as tolerated.
•Manage pain with the healthcare provider's guidance.
•Attend follow-up appointments for monitoring and surveillance.
•Seek emotional and psychological support.
•Complete recommended cancer screenings for early detection.
•Address advance care planning.

Hx of Renal Cancer.education:
What is Renal Cancer (Kidney Cancer)?
Renal cancer, or kidney cancer, is cancer that originates in the kidneys — two bean-shaped organs located behind the abdominal organs on either side of the spine. The most common type of kidney cancer in adults is renal cell carcinoma (RCC), which accounts for about 90% of all kidney cancers and typically begins in the lining of tiny tubes in the kidney (proximal convoluted tubules). Kidney cancer is among the top 10 most common cancers in the United States. For individuals with a history of renal cancer, ongoing surveillance is critical because recurrence can occur months to years after initial treatment, with the highest risk during the first five years. The kidneys play vital roles in filtering waste and excess fluid from the blood, regulating blood pressure, producing hormones that stimulate red blood cell production, and activating vitamin D for bone health. When one kidney is removed (nephrectomy) or partially removed as part of cancer treatment, the remaining kidney tissue must compensate for the lost function, making protection of remaining kidney function especially important. Risk factors for kidney cancer include smoking, obesity, high blood pressure, a family history of kidney cancer, certain genetic conditions (Von Hippel-Lindau disease), long-term dialysis, and workplace exposure to certain chemicals. Surveillance after treatment typically includes regular imaging studies, laboratory work, and clinical examinations on a schedule determined by the oncologist and urologist.

Signs and Symptoms (of recurrence or ongoing issues):
•Blood in the urine (hematuria)
•Persistent pain in the side, back, or abdomen
•A lump or mass in the side or abdomen
•Unexplained weight loss
•Fatigue

•High blood pressure
•Family history of kidney cancer
•Certain genetic conditions (Von Hippel-Lindau disease)
•Long-term dialysis
•Exposure to certain chemicals
•Older age
•Male sex

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the surveillance schedule recommended by the oncologist (imaging, labs).
•Take prescribed medications as directed.
•Monitor remaining kidney function with regular lab work.
•Maintain blood pressure within the recommended range.
•Maintain a healthy weight.
•Stop smoking.
•Stay physically active as tolerated.
•Report new or recurring symptoms immediately.
•Keep all scheduled oncology, urology, nephrology, and PCP appointments.

Laryngeal Cancer.education:
What is Laryngeal Cancer?
Laryngeal cancer is cancer that forms in the tissues of the larynx (voice box), a short passageway in the throat that connects the back of the nose and mouth to the trachea (windpipe) and esophagus. The larynx plays essential roles in breathing, swallowing (protecting the airway from food and liquid aspiration), and speech (producing voice through the vibration of the vocal cords). Most laryngeal cancers are squamous cell carcinomas that develop from the thin, flat cells lining the inside of the larynx. The cancer can occur in three regions: the supraglottis (above the vocal cords), the glottis (the vocal cords themselves, where most laryngeal cancers begin), and the subglottis (below the vocal cords). The combined use of tobacco and alcohol dramatically increases the risk — together they are responsible for the majority of laryngeal cancer cases, with their combined effect being multiplicative rather than simply additive. Other risk factors include HPV infection, occupational exposure to asbestos and certain chemicals, GERD, poor nutrition, and older age. Treatment depends on the size, location, and stage of the cancer and may include radiation therapy, surgery (which may involve partial or total removal of the larynx), chemotherapy, or combinations. Total laryngectomy results in permanent loss of the natural voice, requiring alternative communication methods such as an electrolarynx, tracheoesophageal puncture, or esophageal speech. Speech therapy and swallowing therapy are often essential components of rehabilitation.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Persistent hoarseness or voice changes
•Sore throat that does not improve
•Difficulty or pain when swallowing
•Ear pain
•A lump or mass in the neck
•Persistent cough
•Difficulty breathing or noisy breathing (stridor)
•Unintended weight loss
•Bad breath

Risk Factors:
•Tobacco use (strongest risk factor)
•Heavy alcohol use
•Combined tobacco and alcohol use (greatly increases risk)
•HPV infection
•Older age
•Male sex
•Poor nutrition
•Exposure to certain workplace chemicals (asbestos, paint fumes)
•GERD

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the treatment plan from the oncology team (surgery, radiation, chemotherapy).
•Take prescribed medications as directed.
•Attend speech therapy if voice changes occur after treatment.
•Follow swallowing therapy recommendations.
•Maintain adequate nutrition, using modified diets or feeding tubes if needed.
•Stop smoking and avoid alcohol.
•Attend all follow-up appointments for surveillance.
•Report new or recurring symptoms promptly.
•Seek emotional and psychological support.

Skin Cancer.education:
What is Skin Cancer?
Skin cancer is the abnormal, uncontrolled growth of skin cells, most commonly caused by cumulative damage from ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun or tanning beds. Skin cancer is by far the most common type of cancer, with more cases diagnosed each year than all other cancers combined. There are three main types: basal cell carcinoma (the most common, arising from basal cells in the lowest layer of the epidermis, typically slow-growing and rarely spreads), squamous cell carcinoma (arising from squamous cells in the upper layers of the epidermis, can spread if untreated), and melanoma (arising from melanocytes, the pigment-producing cells, and the most dangerous form because of its ability to spread rapidly to other organs). Early detection is crucial for all types, particularly melanoma, where the five-year survival rate is over 99% when caught early but drops significantly once it has spread. The ABCDE rule helps identify suspicious moles: Asymmetry, irregular Borders, uneven Color, Diameter larger than 6mm, and Evolving (changing) appearance. Risk factors include excessive UV exposure, history of sunburns (especially blistering burns), fair skin/light hair/light eyes, many moles, family or personal history of skin cancer, weakened immune system, and older age. Prevention centers on sun protection: broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen, protective clothing, seeking shade during peak UV hours (10am-4pm), and avoiding tanning beds. Regular skin self-examinations and annual dermatologist visits are recommended for early detection.

Signs and Symptoms:
•A new growth, spot, or bump that is getting larger
•A sore that does not heal within a few weeks
•A spot or sore that itches, hurts, scabs, crusts, or bleeds
•A mole that changes in size, shape, color, or texture
•A mole with irregular borders, uneven color, or asymmetry
•A shiny, waxy, or pearly bump
•A flat, flesh-colored or brown scar-like lesion
•A firm, red nodule

ABCDE Rule for Melanoma:
•A – Asymmetry: one half does not match the other
•B – Border: edges are irregular or blurred
•C – Color: color is uneven or includes shades of brown, black, pink, red, white, or blue
•D – Diameter: larger than 6 mm (size of a pencil eraser)
•E – Evolving: the spot is changing in size, shape, or color

Risk Factors:
•Excessive UV exposure (sun, tanning beds)
•History of sunburns, especially blistering sunburns
•Fair skin, light hair, and light eyes
•Many moles or atypical moles
•Family history of skin cancer
•Personal history of skin cancer
•Weakened immune system
•Older age
•Exposure to certain chemicals

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the dermatologist's and oncologist's treatment plan.
•Perform monthly skin self-examinations.
•Protect skin from UV exposure (sunscreen SPF 30+, protective clothing, shade).
•Avoid tanning beds.
•Attend regular dermatology appointments for skin checks.
•Report any new, changing, or suspicious skin lesions promptly.
•Keep all follow-up appointments for surveillance.

HIV/AIDS.education:
What is HIV/AIDS?
HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) is a virus that attacks and progressively destroys the body's immune system, specifically targeting CD4+ T cells (also called T-helper cells or CD4 cells), which are white blood cells that play a central role in coordinating the immune response to infections. As HIV destroys these cells, the immune system becomes increasingly weakened, leaving the body vulnerable to opportunistic infections and certain cancers that a healthy immune system would normally prevent. If left untreated, HIV infection progresses through three stages: acute infection (flu-like illness 2-4 weeks after exposure with very high viral load), chronic HIV infection (a prolonged period that may last a decade or more with gradual immune decline, often without obvious symptoms), and AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome), the most advanced stage, defined by a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³ or the development of certain opportunistic infections or cancers. With modern antiretroviral therapy (ART), people with HIV who are diagnosed early and take their medications consistently can achieve viral suppression (undetectable viral load), maintain healthy immune function, have a near-normal life expectancy, and — crucially — cannot sexually transmit the virus to others (Undetectable = Untransmittable, or U=U). ART does not cure HIV but effectively controls it, making daily adherence to medication essential. Prevention strategies include PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis) for HIV-negative individuals at risk, consistent condom use, and never sharing needles.

Signs and Symptoms:
Early HIV infection:
•Flu-like symptoms 2-4 weeks after infection (fever, chills, rash, night sweats, muscle aches, sore throat, fatigue, swollen lymph nodes, mouth ulcers)
•Some people may have no symptoms for years

Progressive HIV/AIDS:
•Rapid weight loss
•Recurring fever or night sweats
•Extreme fatigue
•Prolonged swelling of lymph nodes
•Chronic diarrhea
•Sores of the mouth, anus, or genitals
•Pneumonia
•Memory loss and neurological disorders
•Skin rashes or blotches
•Opportunistic infections

Risk Factors:
•Unprotected sexual contact
•Sharing needles or syringes
•Occupational exposure to infected blood
•Mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy, birth, or breastfeeding
•Blood transfusion (rare in the US due to screening)
•Having other sexually transmitted infections

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take antiretroviral therapy (ART) exactly as prescribed, every day, without missing doses.
•Do not stop or change ART without consulting the infectious disease specialist.
•Complete all recommended laboratory tests (viral load, CD4 count, resistance testing).
•Attend all scheduled infectious disease and PCP appointments.
•Practice safer sex and use condoms.
•Do not share needles.
•Receive recommended vaccinations.
•Maintain a healthy diet and stay physically active.
•Avoid smoking and limit alcohol.
•Report new symptoms, side effects, or signs of infection promptly.
•Seek mental health support as needed.
•Disclose HIV status to healthcare providers and sexual partners.

Pulmonary Hypertension.education:
What is Pulmonary Hypertension?
Pulmonary hypertension is a serious condition in which the blood pressure in the arteries of the lungs (pulmonary arteries) is abnormally elevated. This increased pressure makes the right side of the heart work much harder to pump blood through the lungs, and over time the right ventricle can weaken and fail (right heart failure). Pulmonary hypertension can develop as a primary condition (pulmonary arterial hypertension) or can result from other diseases and conditions, including left-sided heart disease, chronic lung diseases such as COPD or pulmonary fibrosis, blood clots in the lungs, sleep apnea, connective tissue disorders, congenital heart defects, liver disease, and HIV infection. Symptoms often develop gradually and may be attributed to other conditions, delaying diagnosis. As the disease progresses, even simple activities like walking or climbing stairs can become difficult. Pulmonary hypertension is a chronic condition that requires ongoing medical management, including specialized medications that help relax and widen the pulmonary arteries, supplemental oxygen if needed, sodium and fluid restriction, regular monitoring, and in some cases, surgical interventions or transplant evaluation.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Shortness of breath, especially with physical activity
•Fatigue or weakness
•Dizziness or fainting (syncope)
•Chest pain or pressure
•Swelling (edema) of the ankles, legs, or abdomen
•Rapid heartbeat or palpitations
•Bluish color of the lips or skin (cyanosis)
•Decreased exercise tolerance

Risk Factors:
•Left-sided heart disease such as heart failure or valve disease
•Chronic lung diseases such as COPD, emphysema, or pulmonary fibrosis
•Sleep apnea
•Blood clots in the lungs (chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension)
•Connective tissue diseases such as scleroderma or lupus
•Congenital heart defects
•Family history of pulmonary hypertension
•Living at high altitudes
•Certain medications or illegal drug use
•HIV infection
•Liver disease (portal hypertension)

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take all prescribed medications as directed, including vasodilators, endothelin receptor antagonists, phosphodiesterase inhibitors, or other pulmonary hypertension-specific therapies.
•Use supplemental oxygen if prescribed.
•Follow sodium and fluid restrictions as directed by the healthcare provider.
•Stay physically active as tolerated and approved by the healthcare provider; participate in pulmonary rehabilitation if recommended.
•Weigh yourself daily and report sudden weight gain.
•Receive recommended vaccinations, including influenza and pneumococcal vaccines.
•Avoid pregnancy if advised by the healthcare provider, as it can be life-threatening with pulmonary hypertension.
•Avoid high altitudes unless discussed with the healthcare provider.
•Keep all scheduled cardiology, pulmonology, and PCP appointments.
•Report new or worsening symptoms promptly.

Bronchiectasis.education:
What is Bronchiectasis?
Bronchiectasis is a chronic lung condition in which the bronchial tubes (airways) become permanently widened, damaged, and thickened due to repeated cycles of infection and inflammation. The structural damage prevents the airways from effectively clearing mucus, creating an environment where bacteria thrive and cause recurrent infections, which in turn cause further airway damage — a destructive cycle that progressively worsens lung function. Bronchiectasis can develop as a result of severe or recurrent respiratory infections (pneumonia, tuberculosis, whooping cough), cystic fibrosis, immune system deficiencies, chronic aspiration of stomach contents, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, or airway obstruction. In many cases, the underlying cause is not identified. Daily management is intensive and revolves around airway clearance techniques — physical maneuvers, devices, and therapies designed to help mobilize and clear the excess mucus from the lungs. Prompt treatment of respiratory infections with antibiotics, regular use of prescribed nebulized medications, exercise, vaccinations, and close follow-up with a pulmonologist are all essential components of managing bronchiectasis.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Chronic cough that produces large amounts of mucus (sputum) daily
•Mucus that may be thick, discolored, or foul-smelling
•Shortness of breath
•Wheezing
•Recurrent respiratory infections
•Coughing up blood (hemoptysis)
•Chest pain
•Fatigue
•Clubbing of the fingertips (in advanced cases)

Risk Factors:
•History of severe or recurrent lung infections (pneumonia, tuberculosis, whooping cough)
•Cystic fibrosis
•Immune system deficiencies
•Chronic aspiration of food or stomach acid
•Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA)
•Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
•Autoimmune or connective tissue diseases
•Primary ciliary dyskinesia
•Airway obstruction (tumor, foreign body)

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed medications as directed, including antibiotics, bronchodilators, and mucus-thinning agents.
•Perform airway clearance techniques daily as directed by the healthcare provider or respiratory therapist.
•Use prescribed nebulizer treatments or inhaled medications consistently.
•Stay well-hydrated to help thin mucus.
•Stay physically active as tolerated.
•Receive recommended vaccinations, including influenza, pneumococcal, and COVID-19 vaccines.
•Avoid smoking and exposure to lung irritants.
•Seek prompt treatment for respiratory infections.
•Keep all scheduled pulmonology and PCP appointments.
•Report changes in mucus color, volume, or consistency, or worsening symptoms.

Emphysema.education:
What is Emphysema?
Emphysema is a chronic, progressive lung condition classified under chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). In emphysema, the tiny air sacs (alveoli) at the ends of the airways in the lungs are gradually destroyed. These air sacs are where the critical exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide takes place. As the alveolar walls break down, the many small air sacs merge into larger, less efficient spaces, dramatically reducing the surface area available for gas exchange and trapping stale air in the lungs. This makes it increasingly difficult to get enough oxygen into the bloodstream and to expel carbon dioxide. The overwhelming cause of emphysema is long-term cigarette smoking, which triggers chronic inflammation and destruction of lung tissue. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, a genetic condition, can also cause emphysema, particularly in younger individuals. The lung damage from emphysema is irreversible, but quitting smoking is the single most important step to slow progression. Treatment focuses on relieving symptoms, improving exercise capacity, and preventing complications through bronchodilator and steroid inhalers, pulmonary rehabilitation, supplemental oxygen, and vaccinations.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Shortness of breath, especially with activity (gradually worsens over time)
•Chronic cough
•Wheezing
•Chest tightness or barrel-shaped chest
•Fatigue
•Reduced exercise tolerance
•Unintended weight loss (in advanced cases)
•Bluish discoloration of the lips or fingernails (cyanosis)

Risk Factors:
•Smoking (most significant risk factor)
•Long-term exposure to secondhand smoke
•Occupational exposure to dust, fumes, or chemical vapors
•Air pollution
•Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (a genetic condition)
•Older age
•History of childhood respiratory infections

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Stop smoking and avoid exposure to lung irritants.
•Take prescribed medications as directed, including bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids, and other COPD medications.
•Use supplemental oxygen if prescribed.
•Participate in pulmonary rehabilitation if recommended.
•Stay physically active as tolerated.
•Practice breathing techniques such as pursed-lip breathing and diaphragmatic breathing.
•Receive recommended vaccinations, including influenza, pneumococcal, and COVID-19 vaccines.
•Maintain good nutrition and a healthy weight.
•Seek prompt treatment for respiratory infections.
•Keep all scheduled pulmonology and PCP appointments.

Thyroid Nodules.education:
What are Thyroid Nodules?
Thyroid nodules are growths or lumps that form within the thyroid gland, a butterfly-shaped gland located in the front of the neck that produces hormones regulating metabolism, heart rate, and body temperature. Thyroid nodules are very common — studies suggest that up to half of all adults have at least one nodule detectable by ultrasound, though most are small and never cause problems. The vast majority of thyroid nodules (more than 90%) are benign (noncancerous). However, a small percentage may be cancerous, which is why evaluation with ultrasound and, when indicated, fine-needle aspiration biopsy is important. Some nodules can grow large enough to cause a visible neck swelling, difficulty swallowing, or a sensation of pressure in the throat. A small number of nodules become "hot" or overactive, producing excess thyroid hormone and causing symptoms of hyperthyroidism such as rapid heartbeat, weight loss, nervousness, and tremor. Management depends on the nodule's size, characteristics, biopsy results, and whether it is causing symptoms or hormone overproduction. Options range from watchful waiting with periodic ultrasound monitoring to surgery (thyroidectomy) or radioactive iodine treatment.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Most thyroid nodules cause no symptoms and are found incidentally during a physical exam or imaging study
•A visible or palpable lump in the front of the neck
•Difficulty swallowing or a feeling of fullness in the throat
•Difficulty breathing if the nodule is large
•Hoarseness or voice changes
•Neck pain
•If the nodule produces excess thyroid hormone, symptoms of hyperthyroidism may occur (rapid heartbeat, weight loss, nervousness, tremor, increased sweating)

Risk Factors:
•Being female
•Older age
•History of radiation exposure to the head or neck
•Family history of thyroid nodules or thyroid cancer
•Iodine deficiency
•Hashimoto's thyroiditis or other thyroid conditions
•Certain genetic syndromes

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the healthcare provider's recommendations for monitoring with regular thyroid ultrasounds and blood tests.
•Take thyroid hormone medication as prescribed if indicated.
•Complete fine-needle aspiration biopsy if recommended by the healthcare provider.
•Report any changes in the size of the nodule, new difficulty swallowing or breathing, hoarseness, or neck pain.
•Discuss the need for surgery (thyroidectomy) with the healthcare provider if the nodule is large, suspicious, or causing symptoms.
•Keep all scheduled endocrinology and PCP appointments.
•Complete recommended thyroid function laboratory tests (TSH, free T4) as ordered.

Diverticulitis.education:
What is Diverticulitis?
Diverticulitis occurs when small, bulging pouches (diverticula) that have formed in the walls of the colon become inflamed or infected. Diverticula are extremely common, particularly after age 40 — a condition called diverticulosis. Most people with diverticulosis never develop symptoms. However, when one or more of these pouches become inflamed, the condition becomes diverticulitis, which can range from mild inflammation treated with rest and antibiotics to severe, complicated disease involving abscess formation, perforation (a tear in the colon wall), peritonitis (infection of the abdominal cavity), fistulas, or bowel obstruction. Acute diverticulitis typically causes significant lower left abdominal pain, fever, and changes in bowel habits. The exact cause of diverticulitis is not fully understood, but it is believed to involve a combination of increased pressure within the colon, changes in the gut microbiome, and possibly micro-perforations in the diverticula. A low-fiber diet has long been considered a risk factor, as fiber helps keep stools soft and reduces pressure in the colon. Other risk factors include obesity, smoking, lack of physical activity, certain medications (NSAIDs, opioids), and aging. After recovery from an acute episode, a high-fiber diet (25-35 grams per day) is recommended to help prevent recurrence.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Pain in the lower left side of the abdomen (most common)
•Fever and chills
•Nausea and vomiting
•Changes in bowel habits (constipation or diarrhea)
•Abdominal tenderness
•Bloating
•Rectal bleeding (less common)
•Urinary symptoms if the inflamed area is near the bladder

Risk Factors:
•Older age (especially over 40)
•Low-fiber diet
•Obesity
•Smoking
•Lack of physical activity
•Certain medications (NSAIDs, steroids, opioids)
•Family history of diverticular disease

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed antibiotics as directed during acute episodes.
•Follow the healthcare provider's dietary recommendations during and after acute episodes.
•Increase dietary fiber gradually when recommended by the healthcare provider.
•Stay well-hydrated.
•Stay physically active.
•Maintain a healthy weight.
•Avoid smoking.
•Complete recommended imaging and follow-up appointments.
•Report recurring abdominal pain, fever, or changes in bowel habits.
•Keep all scheduled gastroenterology and PCP appointments.

GI Bleed.education:
What is a Gastrointestinal (GI) Bleed?
A gastrointestinal bleed is any bleeding that occurs within the gastrointestinal tract, from the esophagus to the rectum. GI bleeding is not a disease itself but a symptom of an underlying condition. It can range from occult bleeding (small amounts detectable only through laboratory testing) to massive, life-threatening hemorrhage. Upper GI bleeds originate above the ligament of Treitz (esophagus, stomach, or duodenum) and commonly present as vomiting blood (hematemesis) or black, tarry stools (melena). Lower GI bleeds originate from the small intestine, colon, or rectum and typically present as bright red blood from the rectum (hematochezia). Common causes of upper GI bleeding include peptic ulcer disease, esophageal varices (often from cirrhosis), gastritis, and esophagitis. Common causes of lower GI bleeding include diverticular disease, hemorrhoids, inflammatory bowel disease, colorectal polyps, and colorectal cancer. Risk factors include the use of NSAIDs, anticoagulants or antiplatelet medications, heavy alcohol use, Helicobacter pylori infection, liver disease, and older age. GI bleeding requires prompt medical evaluation, as significant blood loss can lead to anemia, hypotension, shock, and death. Treatment depends on the cause and severity and may include endoscopic intervention, medications, blood transfusions, and in some cases, surgery.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Vomiting blood (bright red or dark, coffee-ground appearance)
•Black, tarry stools (melena)
•Bright red blood in the stool or from the rectum (hematochezia)
•Abdominal pain or cramping
•Weakness, dizziness, or lightheadedness
•Fatigue
•Pale skin
•Shortness of breath
•Rapid heartbeat
•Decreased urine output
•Fainting

Risk Factors:
•Peptic ulcer disease
•Use of NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin)
•Anticoagulant or antiplatelet medications
•Esophageal varices (often from liver disease or cirrhosis)
•Inflammatory bowel disease
•Diverticular disease
•Hemorrhoids or anal fissures
•Cancer of the GI tract
•Gastritis or esophagitis
•Heavy alcohol use
•Older age
•History of prior GI bleed

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take all prescribed medications as directed.
•Avoid NSAIDs unless approved by the healthcare provider.
•Take prescribed proton pump inhibitors or other acid-reducing medications if indicated.
•Avoid alcohol.
•Report any signs of bleeding (blood in stool, black stools, vomiting blood) immediately.
•Follow dietary recommendations from the healthcare provider.
•Complete recommended endoscopy, colonoscopy, or other diagnostic procedures.
•If on anticoagulant therapy, follow the healthcare provider's instructions carefully and complete required blood tests.
•Keep all scheduled gastroenterology and PCP appointments.
