Gallstones.education:
What are Gallstones?
Gallstones are hard, pebble-like deposits that form inside the gallbladder, a small pear-shaped organ beneath the liver that stores and concentrates bile — a digestive fluid produced by the liver to help digest fats. Gallstones can range in size from as small as a grain of sand to as large as a golf ball, and a person may develop a single large stone, hundreds of tiny stones, or a combination. There are two main types: cholesterol stones (the most common, accounting for about 80% of gallstones, formed when bile contains too much cholesterol) and pigment stones (formed when bile contains too much bilirubin). Most people with gallstones have no symptoms ("silent gallstones") and never require treatment. However, when a gallstone becomes lodged in a bile duct, it can cause sudden, intense pain in the upper right abdomen (biliary colic), often triggered by fatty meals. Complications of gallstones include inflammation of the gallbladder (cholecystitis), infection, blockage of the common bile duct (choledocholithiasis) causing jaundice, and blockage of the pancreatic duct causing acute pancreatitis. Risk factors include being female, age over 40, obesity, rapid weight loss, pregnancy, a high-fat/high-cholesterol/low-fiber diet, family history, diabetes, and certain medications. The most common treatment for symptomatic gallstones is surgical removal of the gallbladder (cholecystectomy), typically performed laparoscopically.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Many people with gallstones have no symptoms (silent gallstones)
•Sudden, intense pain in the upper right abdomen or center of the abdomen (biliary colic)
•Pain that radiates to the right shoulder or back between the shoulder blades
•Nausea and vomiting
•Fever and chills (if infection is present)
•Yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice)
•Clay-colored stools
•Dark urine
•Bloating or indigestion, especially after fatty meals

Risk Factors:
•Being female
•Age 40 or older
•Overweight or obesity
•Rapid weight loss or crash dieting
•Pregnancy
•Family history of gallstones
•High-fat, high-cholesterol, low-fiber diet
•Diabetes
•Certain medications (hormone therapy, cholesterol-lowering drugs)
•Native American or Hispanic descent
•Liver disease

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the healthcare provider's treatment recommendations.
•If surgery (cholecystectomy) is recommended, follow pre- and post-operative instructions.
•Follow dietary recommendations, especially reducing fat intake if symptomatic.
•Maintain a healthy weight; avoid rapid weight loss or crash diets.
•Report recurrent abdominal pain, fever, jaundice, or changes in stool color.
•Complete recommended imaging and laboratory tests.
•Keep all scheduled gastroenterology, surgery, and PCP appointments.

Dysphagia.education:
What is Dysphagia?
Dysphagia is difficulty swallowing — meaning it takes more time, effort, or multiple attempts to move food or liquid from the mouth to the stomach. Swallowing is a complex process involving over 30 muscles and multiple nerves, coordinated by the brain. When any part of this system is impaired, dysphagia can result. There are two main types: oropharyngeal dysphagia (difficulty initiating a swallow, often caused by neurological conditions such as stroke, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, or ALS) and esophageal dysphagia (the sensation of food sticking in the throat or chest, often caused by structural abnormalities, strictures, tumors, or motility disorders). Dysphagia is common in older adults, affecting an estimated 15% of the elderly population, and is present in up to 65% of stroke patients. The most serious complication of dysphagia is aspiration — when food, liquid, or saliva enters the airway and lungs instead of the esophagus — which can lead to aspiration pneumonia, a potentially life-threatening infection. Other consequences include dehydration, malnutrition, weight loss, and social isolation from fear or embarrassment during meals. Proper evaluation by a speech-language pathologist is essential to determine the safest diet texture and liquid consistency, develop swallowing strategies, and guide rehabilitation exercises.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Difficulty initiating a swallow
•Food or liquid getting stuck in the throat or chest
•Pain when swallowing (odynophagia)
•Coughing or choking during or after eating or drinking
•Bringing food back up (regurgitation)
•Recurrent heartburn
•Drooling
•Hoarseness
•Sensation of a lump in the throat
•Unintended weight loss
•Recurrent pneumonia (from aspiration)
•Avoidance of certain foods due to difficulty swallowing

Risk Factors:
•Neurological conditions (stroke, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, ALS, dementia)
•Head and neck cancer or radiation therapy
•Esophageal conditions (strictures, tumors, eosinophilic esophagitis)
•Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)
•Aging and muscle weakness
•Surgery involving the head, neck, or esophagus
•Certain medications that cause dry mouth or esophageal injury

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the speech-language pathologist's and healthcare provider's swallowing recommendations.
•Follow the prescribed diet texture and liquid consistency (regular, mechanical soft, pureed, thickened liquids).
•Sit upright during meals and remain upright for at least 30 minutes after eating.
•Eat slowly and take small bites and sips.
•Avoid talking while eating.
•Follow swallowing exercises as prescribed.
•Maintain adequate nutrition and hydration.
•Report new or worsening difficulty swallowing, choking, coughing during meals, or unintended weight loss.
•Keep all scheduled speech therapy, gastroenterology, and PCP appointments.

Amputation.education:
What is Amputation Aftercare?
Amputation is the surgical removal of a limb or part of a limb. Common reasons include peripheral vascular disease, diabetes-related complications, trauma, infection, or cancer. After amputation, ongoing care is essential for healing, rehabilitation, and maintaining quality of life.

Signs and Symptoms to Monitor After Amputation:
•Pain at the surgical site or phantom limb pain (sensation of pain in the limb that was removed)
•Swelling of the residual limb (stump)
•Skin changes, redness, or breakdown on the residual limb
•Wound drainage or signs of infection
•Emotional changes including grief, depression, or anxiety
•Difficulty with balance or mobility
•Phantom limb sensations (feeling as if the removed limb is still present)

Risk Factors for Amputation:
•Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) or peripheral vascular disease (PVD)
•Diabetes with poorly controlled blood sugar
•Non-healing wounds or ulcers
•Severe infection (gangrene, osteomyelitis)
•Severe trauma or crush injury
•Cancer involving the limb
•Smoking

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow wound care instructions exactly as directed by the healthcare provider.
•Keep the residual limb clean, dry, and properly bandaged or wrapped.
•Inspect the residual limb daily for redness, swelling, skin breakdown, blisters, or drainage.
•Participate in physical and occupational therapy as recommended.
•Use prescribed prosthetic devices and follow the prosthetist's fitting and care instructions.
•Perform prescribed exercises to maintain strength, flexibility, and range of motion.
•Position the residual limb as directed to prevent contractures.
•Manage pain with prescribed medications and non-drug strategies.
•Discuss phantom limb pain management with the healthcare provider.
•Address emotional and mental health needs; seek counseling or support groups.
•Manage underlying conditions (diabetes, vascular disease) to prevent complications in the remaining limb.
•Keep all scheduled surgery, rehabilitation, prosthetics, and PCP appointments.

Carpal Tunnel Syndrome.education:
What is Carpal Tunnel Syndrome?
Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is one of the most common peripheral nerve disorders, caused by compression of the median nerve as it passes through the carpal tunnel — a narrow, rigid passageway of bone and ligament at the base of the hand on the palm side of the wrist. The median nerve controls sensation to the thumb, index, middle, and ring fingers and powers some small muscles at the base of the thumb. When the tissues surrounding the tendons in the carpal tunnel swell or thicken (tenosynovitis), they compress the nerve, causing numbness, tingling, weakness, and pain in the affected hand. CTS affects an estimated 3-6% of the general adult population and is more common in women, likely due to smaller carpal tunnel anatomy. Contributing factors include repetitive hand and wrist motions, awkward wrist positioning, vibrating tools, pregnancy, diabetes, thyroid disease, rheumatoid arthritis, obesity, and fluid retention. Symptoms often begin gradually, frequently worsen at night, and may progress to constant numbness, grip weakness, and muscle wasting at the base of the thumb if untreated. Treatment begins conservatively with wrist splinting (especially at night), activity modification, ergonomic improvements, and anti-inflammatory measures, progressing to corticosteroid injections and ultimately surgical release of the transverse carpal ligament if conservative management fails.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Numbness, tingling, or burning in the thumb, index, middle, and ring fingers
•Pain in the hand, wrist, or forearm
•Weakness in the hand, especially difficulty gripping objects
•Dropping objects
•Sensation of swollen fingers even when no swelling is visible
•Symptoms often worse at night or upon waking
•Symptoms may worsen with activities that involve flexing the wrist (driving, reading, typing)
•In advanced cases, loss of sensation and muscle wasting at the base of the thumb

Risk Factors:
•Repetitive hand and wrist motions (typing, assembly line work)
•Wrist injuries or fractures
•Being female (women are more likely to develop CTS)
•Pregnancy
•Diabetes
•Rheumatoid arthritis
•Hypothyroidism
•Obesity
•Fluid retention
•Older age

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Wear a wrist splint as prescribed, especially at night.
•Take prescribed medications (anti-inflammatory drugs, corticosteroid injections) as directed.
•Modify activities that aggravate symptoms; take frequent breaks from repetitive hand motions.
•Perform prescribed hand and wrist stretching exercises.
•Apply cold packs to reduce swelling if recommended.
•Maintain proper wrist positioning during work and daily activities.
•Use ergonomic tools and workstation modifications.
•Discuss surgical options (carpal tunnel release) with the healthcare provider if conservative treatment does not provide relief.
•Manage underlying conditions that may contribute to CTS (diabetes, thyroid disease).
•Keep all scheduled orthopedic, neurology, and PCP appointments.

Spondylosis.education:
What is Spondylosis?
Spondylosis is a general term for age-related degenerative changes (wear and tear) of the spinal discs, joints, and vertebrae — essentially osteoarthritis of the spine. It is an extremely common condition, with imaging studies showing degenerative changes in the majority of people over age 60, though many have no symptoms. Spondylosis can occur in any region of the spine but most frequently affects the cervical spine (neck) and lumbar spine (lower back), which bear the most weight and undergo the most movement. As the spine degenerates, discs lose height and flexibility, bone spurs (osteophytes) form along the edges of vertebrae, the facet joints that connect vertebrae become arthritic, and the ligaments that stabilize the spine may thicken. These changes can narrow the spinal canal (spinal stenosis) or the openings where nerves exit the spine (foraminal stenosis), potentially compressing the spinal cord or nerve roots. Cervical spondylosis can cause neck pain, stiffness, headaches, and if nerves are compressed, pain, numbness, or weakness radiating into the arms and hands. In severe cases, cervical spondylotic myelopathy (compression of the spinal cord) can affect balance, coordination, and hand dexterity. Lumbar spondylosis can cause back pain, stiffness, and sciatica. Treatment is typically conservative including physical therapy, pain management, maintaining mobility, and ergonomic modifications, with surgery reserved for cases involving significant nerve compression.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Stiffness and pain in the neck or back
•Pain that worsens with activity or prolonged sitting/standing
•Headaches (cervical spondylosis)
•Grinding or popping sensation with movement
•Numbness, tingling, or weakness in the arms, hands, legs, or feet if nerves are compressed
•Difficulty with balance or coordination (in severe cervical cases)
•Reduced range of motion in the spine
•Muscle spasms
•Some people have no symptoms

Risk Factors:
•Aging (most significant factor)
•Prior spinal injuries
•Repetitive stress on the spine from occupation or activities
•Obesity
•Smoking
•Genetic predisposition
•Sedentary lifestyle
•Heavy lifting or manual labor

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed pain medications, anti-inflammatories, or muscle relaxants as directed.
•Participate in physical therapy to improve flexibility, strength, and posture.
•Stay physically active with low-impact exercises such as walking, swimming, or yoga.
•Maintain proper posture and body mechanics.
•Use ergonomic supports when sitting or sleeping.
•Apply heat or cold therapy as recommended.
•Maintain a healthy weight to reduce stress on the spine.
•Stop smoking.
•Consider epidural steroid injections or surgical options if recommended by the healthcare provider.
•Keep all scheduled orthopedic, neurosurgery, and PCP appointments.

Wound Care.education:
What is Wound Care?
Wound care is the systematic management and treatment of wounds to promote healing, prevent infection, and minimize complications. Wounds can be acute (surgical incisions, traumatic injuries, burns) or chronic (pressure injuries, diabetic foot ulcers, venous leg ulcers, arterial ulcers). Chronic wounds are defined as wounds that fail to progress through the normal stages of healing in an orderly and timely manner, typically not healing within 30 days. Normal wound healing involves four overlapping phases: hemostasis (blood clotting), inflammation (immune response to clear debris and bacteria), proliferation (new tissue formation), and remodeling (tissue strengthening and maturation). Many factors can impair this process, including poor blood supply, diabetes with uncontrolled blood sugar, infection, malnutrition (particularly protein, vitamin C, vitamin A, and zinc deficiency), smoking, obesity, immunosuppression, advanced age, and prolonged pressure on the skin. Chronic wounds represent a significant healthcare challenge, affecting approximately 6.5 million patients in the United States annually and costing over $25 billion per year to treat. Proper wound care requires a systematic approach that includes thorough assessment, appropriate wound cleansing, selection of appropriate wound dressings (moist wound healing is the current standard), infection prevention and management, optimization of nutrition, management of underlying conditions, offloading pressure, and regular reassessment. Patient and caregiver education on wound care techniques, signs of infection, and when to seek medical attention is essential for successful outcomes.

Signs and Symptoms to Monitor:
•Redness, warmth, or swelling around the wound
•Increased pain or tenderness at the wound site
•Drainage from the wound (clear, yellow, green, or foul-smelling)
•Wound edges that are separating or not closing
•Darkening or discoloration of the wound or surrounding skin
•Fever or chills
•Slow or stalled healing progress
•Numbness around the wound

Risk Factors for Poor Wound Healing:
•Diabetes with poorly controlled blood sugar
•Peripheral vascular disease or poor circulation
•Obesity
•Malnutrition or protein deficiency
•Smoking
•Immunosuppression (medications, medical conditions)
•Older age
•Prolonged immobility or pressure on the skin
•Chronic kidney disease
•Certain medications (corticosteroids, anticoagulants)

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow wound care instructions exactly as directed by the healthcare provider or wound care specialist.
•Keep the wound clean using prescribed cleansing solutions.
•Change dressings at the recommended frequency using the prescribed materials.
•Wash hands thoroughly before and after wound care.
•Monitor the wound daily for signs of infection or changes.
•Keep the wound protected and avoid unnecessary touching.
•Maintain adequate nutrition, especially protein, vitamins A and C, and zinc.
•Keep blood sugar well-controlled if diabetic.
•Avoid smoking, which impairs wound healing.
•Reposition frequently to prevent pressure injuries if mobility is limited.
•Follow activity restrictions as directed (weight-bearing, lifting).
•Keep all scheduled wound care, surgery, and PCP appointments.

Atopic Dermatitis.education:
What is Atopic Dermatitis?
Atopic dermatitis (eczema) is the most common chronic inflammatory skin condition, affecting approximately 31.6 million people in the United States. It is characterized by dry, itchy, and inflamed skin that often appears in patches and tends to flare up periodically before subsiding. Atopic dermatitis is part of the "atopic triad" — a group of allergic conditions that includes eczema, asthma, and hay fever (allergic rhinitis) — and people with atopic dermatitis frequently have or develop one or both of the other conditions. The condition results from a combination of genetic factors (particularly mutations in the filaggrin gene, which is important for skin barrier function), immune system dysregulation (overactive inflammatory response), and environmental triggers. A weakened skin barrier allows moisture to escape and irritants, allergens, and microorganisms to penetrate the skin, triggering inflammation and the intense itch that is the hallmark of the disease. The itch-scratch cycle — where scratching damaged skin causes more inflammation and more itching — can be extremely difficult to break. Atopic dermatitis can significantly affect sleep quality, mental health, self-esteem, and overall quality of life. Treatment follows a stepladder approach: consistent skin hydration with emollients as the foundation, topical anti-inflammatory medications (corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, PDE4 inhibitors), and for moderate to severe cases, systemic therapies including immunomodulators and biologic medications such as dupilumab.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Dry, cracked skin
•Itching, which may be severe, especially at night
•Red to brownish-gray patches on the skin
•Small, raised bumps that may leak fluid when scratched
•Thickened, scaly skin from repeated scratching (lichenification)
•Raw, sensitive, or swollen skin from scratching
•Common locations: hands, feet, ankles, wrists, neck, upper chest, eyelids, inside the bend of elbows and knees, and in infants, the face and scalp

Risk Factors:
•Family history of eczema, allergies, hay fever, or asthma
•Personal history of allergies or asthma
•Childhood onset (most common)
•Living in dry or cold climates
•Living in urban areas
•Exposure to environmental irritants

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Apply prescribed moisturizers (emollients) liberally and frequently, especially after bathing.
•Use prescribed topical medications (corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, PDE4 inhibitors) as directed.
•Take prescribed oral or injectable medications (immunomodulators, biologics) if indicated.
•Bathe in lukewarm water for short periods and pat skin dry gently.
•Avoid known triggers (harsh soaps, fragrances, certain fabrics, allergens, stress, extreme temperatures).
•Use mild, fragrance-free soaps, detergents, and skin care products.
•Wear soft, breathable clothing (cotton).
•Keep fingernails trimmed to reduce skin damage from scratching.
•Use wet wrap therapy if recommended by the healthcare provider.
•Manage stress, which can trigger flares.
•Keep all scheduled dermatology and PCP appointments.

Basal Cell Carcinoma.education:
What is Basal Cell Carcinoma?
Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common type of skin cancer and the most frequently occurring form of all cancers. An estimated 3.6 million cases are diagnosed annually in the United States. BCC arises from the basal cells, which are found in the deepest layer of the outer skin (epidermis). BCC typically grows slowly over months to years and very rarely metastasizes (spreads to distant parts of the body). However, if left untreated, BCC can grow deep into the skin and invade surrounding tissue, causing significant local destruction of skin, cartilage, and bone, particularly when it occurs on the face, nose, ears, or around the eyes. The overwhelming cause of BCC is cumulative ultraviolet (UV) radiation exposure from sunlight or tanning beds, which damages the DNA in skin cells. People with fair skin, light hair, light eyes, a history of sunburns (especially blistering sunburns in childhood), and chronic sun exposure are at highest risk. BCC typically appears as a pearly or waxy bump, a flat flesh-colored or brown scar-like lesion, or a sore that repeatedly bleeds, crusts, and fails to heal. Treatment is highly effective when caught early and may include surgical excision, Mohs micrographic surgery (which offers the highest cure rate for high-risk BCC), cryotherapy, topical medications, or radiation therapy. After diagnosis, regular dermatology follow-up and sun protection are essential, as having one BCC significantly increases the risk of developing additional skin cancers.

Signs and Symptoms:
•A pearly or waxy bump on the face, ears, or neck
•A flat, flesh-colored or brown scar-like lesion on the chest or back
•A sore that bleeds, oozes, crusts, and does not heal, or heals and returns
•A pink growth with a slightly raised, rolled border and a crusted center
•A shiny bump or nodule that is translucent and may have visible blood vessels
•An area that looks like a scar without a known injury

Risk Factors:
•Chronic or excessive sun exposure (UV radiation)
•History of sunburns, especially blistering sunburns
•Fair skin, light hair, and light eyes
•Older age
•Male sex
•History of prior skin cancer
•Use of tanning beds
•Exposure to radiation therapy
•Immunosuppression
•Exposure to arsenic
•Certain genetic conditions (basal cell nevus syndrome)

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the dermatologist's treatment plan (surgical excision, Mohs surgery, cryotherapy, topical treatments, or other therapies).
•Attend regular follow-up skin examinations as recommended.
•Perform monthly skin self-examinations.
•Protect skin from UV exposure: use broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF 30 or higher), wear protective clothing, seek shade, and avoid peak sun hours.
•Avoid tanning beds.
•Report any new, changing, or non-healing skin lesions promptly.
•Keep all scheduled dermatology and PCP appointments.

Medication Induced Coagulopathy.education:
What is Medication Induced Coagulopathy?
Medication induced coagulopathy is a condition in which medications — most commonly anticoagulants (blood thinners) and antiplatelet agents — interfere with the blood's normal ability to form clots. Blood clotting (coagulation) is a complex process involving platelets and clotting factors that work together to stop bleeding. While anticoagulant and antiplatelet medications are prescribed for important therapeutic reasons — preventing harmful blood clots in conditions such as atrial fibrillation, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, mechanical heart valves, and after coronary stent placement — they inherently increase the risk of bleeding. The challenge in managing these medications is maintaining the delicate balance between preventing dangerous clots and avoiding excessive bleeding. Commonly used anticoagulants include warfarin (Coumadin), which works by inhibiting vitamin K-dependent clotting factors and requires regular INR monitoring; direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) such as apixaban (Eliquis), rivaroxaban (Xarelto), and dabigatran (Pradaxa); and injectable heparin and enoxaparin. Antiplatelet agents include aspirin, clopidogrel (Plavix), ticagrelor (Brilinta), and prasugrel (Effient). The risk of bleeding complications is increased by older age, kidney or liver disease, drug interactions, falls, concurrent use of NSAIDs, excessive alcohol use, and inconsistent medication adherence. Patient education about medication adherence, recognizing signs of bleeding, drug and food interactions, the importance of regular monitoring, and when to seek emergency care is critical for safe management.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Easy bruising or bruising that is larger than expected
•Prolonged bleeding from cuts or wounds
•Nosebleeds that are frequent or difficult to stop
•Bleeding gums

Consistent Diet for Anticoagulant Management:
If taking warfarin, maintaining a consistent daily intake of vitamin K is essential for stable anticoagulation. Addison's Disease.education:
What is Addison's Disease?
Addison's disease, also known as primary adrenal insufficiency, is a rare but serious condition in which the adrenal glands — small glands located on top of each kidney — do not produce enough of the hormones cortisol and aldosterone. Cortisol is essential for the body's stress response, blood pressure regulation, metabolism, immune function, and inflammation control. Aldosterone helps regulate the balance of sodium and potassium in the blood, which directly affects blood pressure and fluid balance. Without adequate levels of these hormones, the body cannot respond appropriately to physical stress such as illness, injury, or surgery, which can lead to an adrenal crisis — a life-threatening emergency characterized by severe hypotension, dehydration, and shock. The most common cause of Addison's disease is autoimmune destruction of the adrenal glands, in which the body's immune system mistakenly attacks the adrenal cortex. Other causes include infections (tuberculosis), bleeding into the adrenal glands, cancer that has spread to the adrenals, and surgical removal of the adrenal glands. Treatment involves lifelong hormone replacement therapy with corticosteroids and, in many cases, mineralocorticoids. People with Addison's disease must learn to adjust their medication doses during illness, injury, or surgical procedures (stress dosing) and must carry emergency identification and an injectable corticosteroid kit at all times.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Extreme fatigue and weakness
•Unintended weight loss and decreased appetite
•Darkening of the skin (hyperpigmentation), especially in skin folds, scars, and gums
•Low blood pressure, including dizziness or fainting when standing
•Salt cravings
•Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia)
•Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or abdominal pain
•Muscle or joint pain
•Irritability or depression
•Body hair loss or sexual dysfunction (in women)

Adrenal Crisis (Emergency):
•Severe weakness
•Severe pain in the lower back, abdomen, or legs
•Severe nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea leading to dehydration
•Low blood pressure and loss of consciousness
•High potassium and low sodium levels

Risk Factors:
•Autoimmune disorders (most common cause)
•Tuberculosis
•Other infections affecting the adrenal glands
•Bleeding into the adrenal glands
•Cancer that has spread to the adrenal glands
•Surgical removal of the adrenal glands
•Long-term use of corticosteroids followed by sudden discontinuation
•Family history of autoimmune conditions

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed hormone replacement medications (hydrocortisone, prednisone, or fludrocortisone) exactly as directed.
•Never skip or stop taking medications without consulting the healthcare provider.
•Learn to adjust medication doses during illness, injury, or surgery (stress dosing) as directed by the healthcare provider.
•Carry a medical alert identification card and wear medical alert jewelry.
•Carry an emergency injectable corticosteroid kit and know how to use it.
•Maintain adequate sodium intake as recommended.
•Keep all scheduled endocrinology and PCP appointments.
•Inform all healthcare providers, dentists, and emergency personnel about the diagnosis.
•Report signs of adrenal crisis immediately.
•Receive recommended vaccinations.

Overactive Bladder.education:
What is Overactive Bladder (OAB)?
Overactive bladder is a condition characterized by a sudden, frequent, and difficult-to-control urge to urinate that can significantly affect daily life. OAB occurs when the bladder muscle (detrusor) contracts involuntarily, even when the volume of urine in the bladder is small, creating an urgent need to urinate. It may result in urge incontinence — the involuntary loss of urine immediately following an urgent need. OAB affects an estimated 33 million Americans, though many people do not seek treatment due to embarrassment or the belief that it is a normal part of aging. While OAB is more common in older adults, it is not a normal consequence of aging and effective treatments are available. Contributing factors include neurological conditions (stroke, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease), diabetes, urinary tract infections, hormonal changes after menopause, enlarged prostate, excessive caffeine or alcohol intake, and certain medications. Treatment typically begins with behavioral strategies — bladder retraining, pelvic floor exercises (Kegels), and lifestyle modifications — before advancing to medications (anticholinergics or beta-3 agonists) or more advanced therapies (Botox injections, nerve stimulation) if needed.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Urinary urgency — a sudden, strong need to urinate that is difficult to control
•Frequent urination — needing to urinate more than eight times in 24 hours
•Urge incontinence — involuntary loss of urine immediately following an urgent need to urinate
•Nocturia — waking two or more times during the night to urinate

Risk Factors:
•Older age
•Menopause and estrogen deficiency
•Enlarged prostate (BPH) in men
•Neurological conditions (stroke, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, spinal cord injury)
•Diabetes
•Urinary tract infections
•Pelvic surgery or radiation
•Obesity
•Excessive caffeine or alcohol intake
•Certain medications (diuretics)
•Pregnancy and childbirth
•Weakened pelvic floor muscles

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Practice bladder retraining techniques as directed by the healthcare provider.
•Perform pelvic floor muscle exercises (Kegel exercises) regularly.
•Maintain a bladder diary to track urination patterns, fluid intake, and episodes of urgency or leakage.
•Limit or avoid caffeine and alcohol, which can irritate the bladder.
•Manage fluid intake — drink adequate but not excessive amounts, and limit fluids in the evening.
•Maintain a healthy weight.
•Manage constipation, which can worsen OAB symptoms.
•Take prescribed medications (anticholinergics such as oxybutynin, or beta-3 agonists such as mirabegron) as directed.
•Discuss advanced treatment options (Botox injections, nerve stimulation, surgery) with the healthcare provider if needed.
•Keep all scheduled urology, urogynecology, and PCP appointments.

Bladder Retraining and Kegel.education:
What is Bladder Retraining and Kegel Exercise?
Bladder retraining and Kegel (pelvic floor) exercises are evidence-based behavioral therapies used to improve bladder control and reduce urinary incontinence. They are considered first-line treatments for overactive bladder, urge incontinence, and stress incontinence, and are often recommended before or alongside medication. Bladder retraining works by gradually increasing the intervals between voiding to "retrain" the bladder to hold larger volumes of urine, reducing urgency and frequency. Kegel exercises strengthen the pelvic floor muscles — the group of muscles that support the bladder, uterus, and rectum and control the flow of urine. Weak pelvic floor muscles, which can result from pregnancy and childbirth, surgery, aging, chronic coughing, or obesity, are a major contributing factor to urinary incontinence. When performed correctly and consistently, these exercises can significantly improve or even resolve incontinence symptoms for many people. Both techniques require patience and commitment — improvement typically takes 6 to 12 weeks of consistent daily practice. A healthcare provider, nurse, or pelvic floor physical therapist can help ensure exercises are being performed correctly, as many people inadvertently squeeze the wrong muscles.

Bladder Retraining Instructions:
•Empty your bladder as soon as you get up in the morning. This starts your retraining schedule.
•Go to the bathroom at the specific times you and your healthcare provider have discussed. Wait until your next scheduled time before urinating again.
•Be sure to empty your bladder at each scheduled time, even if you feel no urge to urinate.
•When you have accomplished your initial goal, gradually increase the time between emptying your bladder by 15-minute intervals.
•Try to increase your interval each week.
•If you feel the urge to urinate before your scheduled time, use relaxation techniques: stop and stand still or sit down, take slow deep breaths, squeeze your pelvic floor muscles, and wait until the urge passes before walking slowly to the bathroom.
•It should take between 6 to 12 weeks to accomplish your goal.

Kegel Exercise Instructions:
•To do a Kegel exercise, squeeze the muscles you would use to stop the flow of urine or prevent passing gas.
•Do not tighten the muscles of your abdomen, buttocks, or thighs. Focus only on the pelvic floor muscles.
•To complete one set, squeeze your pelvic floor muscles for a slow count of three, then relax the muscles completely for a slow count of three.
•Do not push the muscles outward during the relaxation phase.
•Repeat 10 times to complete one set (10 squeezes equal one set).
•Perform three sets each day (morning, afternoon, and evening).
•As your muscle strength improves, increase the squeeze and relaxation count to five seconds each.
•Be consistent — results require regular, daily exercise over several weeks.

Signs and Symptoms That May Indicate the Need for Bladder Retraining:
•Frequent urination (more than eight times in 24 hours)
•Sudden, strong urges to urinate
•Urge incontinence (leaking urine before reaching the bathroom)
•Nocturia (waking at night to urinate)
•Stress incontinence (leaking urine with coughing, sneezing, laughing, or exercise)

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the bladder retraining schedule consistently.
•Perform Kegel exercises daily as recommended.
•Keep a bladder diary to track progress.
•Report improvements or difficulties to the healthcare provider.
•Combine bladder retraining and Kegel exercises with other treatments as directed.
•Be patient — improvement typically takes 6 to 12 weeks of consistent practice.
•Keep all scheduled urology, urogynecology, or PCP appointments.

GERD.education:
What is GERD?
Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a chronic digestive condition in which stomach acid and sometimes bile flow backward (reflux) from the stomach into the esophagus — the tube that connects the mouth to the stomach. While occasional acid reflux is common, GERD is diagnosed when reflux occurs frequently (typically more than twice per week) and causes troublesome symptoms or complications. The lower esophageal sphincter (LES), a ring of muscle at the junction of the esophagus and stomach, normally acts as a one-way valve to prevent backflow. In GERD, the LES is weakened or relaxes inappropriately, allowing acidic stomach contents to irritate and damage the esophageal lining. Over time, chronic GERD can lead to esophagitis (inflammation of the esophagus), esophageal strictures (narrowing due to scar tissue), Barrett's esophagus (a precancerous change in the esophageal lining), and in rare cases, esophageal cancer. GERD affects approximately 20% of the U.S. adult population. Contributing factors include obesity, hiatal hernia, pregnancy, smoking, certain foods and beverages, eating large meals or eating late at night, and certain medications. Treatment involves a combination of lifestyle modifications (dietary changes, weight loss, elevating the head of the bed, avoiding late meals) and medications (antacids, H2 receptor blockers, proton pump inhibitors).

Signs and Symptoms:
•Heartburn — a burning sensation in the chest, usually after eating, that may worsen when lying down
•Acid or food coming back into the mouth (regurgitation)
•Sour or bitter taste in the mouth
•Difficulty swallowing
•Chronic cough
•Hoarseness or sore throat
•Feeling like there is a lump in the throat
•Chest pain (non-cardiac)
•Symptoms that worsen after eating or when lying down
•Worsening of asthma symptoms

Risk Factors:
•Obesity or overweight
•Hiatal hernia
•Pregnancy
•Smoking
•Eating large meals or eating late at night
•Certain foods (fatty, fried, spicy, acidic)
•Certain beverages (coffee, alcohol, carbonated drinks)
•Certain medications (aspirin, NSAIDs, some blood pressure medications)
•Connective tissue disorders such as scleroderma
•Delayed stomach emptying

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed medications as directed (antacids, H2 blockers such as famotidine, or proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole).
•Eat smaller, more frequent meals.
•Avoid eating 2-3 hours before bedtime.
•Elevate the head of the bed 6-8 inches if nighttime symptoms occur.
•Maintain a healthy weight.
•Avoid tight-fitting clothing around the waist.
•Stop smoking.
•Limit alcohol intake.
•Identify and avoid personal trigger foods.
•Stay hydrated.
•Manage stress through relaxation techniques and regular exercise.
•Report persistent or worsening symptoms, difficulty swallowing, or unintended weight loss.
•Keep all scheduled gastroenterology and PCP appointments.

Migraine.education:
What is Migraine?
Migraine is a complex neurological condition that causes recurring episodes of moderate to severe headache, typically accompanied by a constellation of neurological and systemic symptoms. Migraine is far more than "just a headache" — it is a disabling condition that affects approximately 12% of the U.S. population, with women being three times more likely to be affected than men. A migraine attack typically progresses through up to four phases: the prodrome (hours to days before the headache, with mood changes, food cravings, fatigue, or yawning), aura (visual disturbances, numbness, or speech changes occurring in about 25% of people with migraine), the headache phase (intense, often one-sided throbbing pain lasting 4-72 hours if untreated, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and extreme sensitivity to light, sound, and smell), and the postdrome (fatigue, difficulty concentrating, and weakness lasting hours to days after the headache resolves). Migraine has a strong genetic component, and triggers vary widely between individuals but commonly include stress, hormonal changes, irregular sleep, skipped meals, dehydration, certain foods and beverages, weather changes, bright or flickering lights, and strong odors. Migraine is a leading cause of disability worldwide. Treatment includes acute medications to stop an attack in progress (triptans, gepants, NSAIDs) and preventive medications to reduce the frequency and severity of attacks (beta-blockers, anticonvulsants, antidepressants, CGRP monoclonal antibodies, Botox injections). Lifestyle management — maintaining regular sleep, meals, hydration, exercise, and stress management — is equally important.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Intense, throbbing, or pulsing headache, often on one side of the head but sometimes on both sides
•Nausea and vomiting
•Sensitivity to light, sound, or smells
•Dizziness or lightheadedness
•Fatigue or weakness
•Visual disturbances (aura), such as flashing lights, zigzag lines, or blind spots
•Numbness or tingling, usually in the face or hands (aura)
•Difficulty concentrating or thinking clearly (brain fog)
•Mood changes, irritability, or depression before or after an attack
•Neck stiffness
•Food cravings or loss of appetite before an attack
•Yawning excessively before an attack (prodromal phase)

Risk Factors:
•Family history of migraine (strong genetic component)
•Being female (women are three times more likely than men to experience migraine)
•Hormonal changes (menstruation, pregnancy, menopause, oral contraceptive use)
•Age (most commonly begins in teens to early twenties)
•Stress
•Sleep disturbances (too much or too little sleep, irregular sleep schedule)
•Certain foods and beverages (alcohol, aged cheeses, chocolate, caffeine, processed foods, foods containing MSG or nitrates)
•Environmental factors (bright or flickering lights, strong smells, loud sounds, weather changes)
•Dehydration
•Skipping meals
•Other medical conditions (depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, sleep disorders, epilepsy)
•Tobacco use

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed medications as directed. Migraine medications may include acute treatments (triptans, NSAIDs, anti-nausea medications, gepants) and preventive treatments (beta-blockers, anticonvulsants, antidepressants, CGRP monoclonal antibodies, or Botox injections).
•Take acute migraine medication at the first sign of an attack for best effectiveness.
•Avoid overusing acute pain medications, which can lead to medication-overuse headache (rebound headache).
•Keep a headache diary or journal to track frequency, duration, triggers, symptoms, and response to treatment.
•Identify and avoid personal migraine triggers.
•Maintain a regular sleep schedule.
•Stay well-hydrated and do not skip meals.
•Manage stress through relaxation techniques, exercise, biofeedback, or cognitive behavioral therapy.
•Stay physically active with regular, moderate exercise as tolerated.
•Rest in a quiet, dark room during an attack.
•Apply cold packs to the forehead or neck if helpful.
•Discuss preventive medication options with the healthcare provider if migraines occur frequently (4 or more days per month), are severe, or significantly interfere with daily life.
•Keep all scheduled neurology and PCP appointments.

Colorectal Cancer.education:
What is Colorectal Cancer?
Colorectal cancer is cancer that develops in the colon (the first and longest part of the large intestine) or the rectum (the lower portion connecting to the anus). It is the third most commonly diagnosed cancer and the second leading cause of cancer death in the United States when men and women are combined. Most colorectal cancers begin as noncancerous growths called polyps that form on the inner lining of the colon or rectum. Over time — usually many years — certain types of polyps (particularly adenomatous polyps) can undergo genetic changes that transform them into cancer. This slow progression from polyp to cancer is what makes screening so valuable, as polyps can be found and removed before they become cancerous. When detected early at a localized stage, the five-year survival rate for colorectal cancer exceeds 90%. However, many people skip recommended screenings, allowing cancers to grow and spread before they are detected. Current guidelines recommend that average-risk adults begin colorectal cancer screening at age 45 through colonoscopy, stool-based tests, or other approved methods. Risk factors include older age, personal or family history of polyps or colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, inherited genetic syndromes (Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis), a diet high in red and processed meats, obesity, physical inactivity, smoking, heavy alcohol use, and type 2 diabetes. Treatment depends on the stage and may include surgical removal, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Changes in bowel habits (diarrhea, constipation, or narrowing of the stool) lasting more than a few days
•Feeling that the bowel does not empty completely
•Rectal bleeding or blood in the stool (bright red or very dark)
•Persistent abdominal discomfort such as cramps, gas, or pain
•Weakness and fatigue
•Unintended weight loss
•Nausea or vomiting
•Iron deficiency anemia without a known cause
•Many people with early colorectal cancer have no symptoms, making screening important

Risk Factors:
•Age 45 or older (risk increases with age)
•Personal history of colorectal polyps or colorectal cancer
•Personal history of inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis)
•Family history of colorectal cancer or polyps
•Inherited genetic syndromes (Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis)
•Diet high in red and processed meats
•Low-fiber diet
•Physical inactivity
•Obesity
•Smoking
•Heavy alcohol use
•Type 2 diabetes
•African American descent (higher incidence and mortality rates)

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the oncology team's treatment plan (surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy).
•Take all prescribed medications as directed.
•Attend all scheduled treatment sessions and follow-up appointments.
•Complete recommended colorectal cancer surveillance (colonoscopies, imaging, CEA blood tests) on schedule.
•Maintain adequate nutrition and hydration, especially during treatment.
•Stay physically active as tolerated.
•Manage treatment side effects with the oncology team's guidance.
•Report new or worsening symptoms promptly.
•Complete age-appropriate colorectal cancer screening as recommended (colonoscopy, stool-based tests).
•Seek emotional and psychological support.
•Address advance care planning.

diet.overview: Colorectal Cancer and Post-Treatment Diet: A balanced, high-fiber diet supports colon health and may help reduce the risk of recurrence. During active treatment, dietary needs may change — smaller, more frequent meals and easily digestible foods may be better tolerated. After treatment, gradually returning to a high-fiber diet promotes healthy bowel function. The oncology team and dietitian can provide individualized guidance.
eat_more: High-fiber foods including fruits, vegetables, whole grains, beans, and legumes
Lean proteins such as fish, poultry, and plant-based proteins
Calcium-rich foods (low-fat dairy, fortified plant milks, leafy greens)
Adequate fluids to support fiber intake and hydration
limit: Red meat (beef, pork, lamb) to no more than 18 ounces per week
Processed meats (bacon, sausage, hot dogs, deli meats)
avoid: Processed meats as much as possible
Raw or undercooked foods during chemotherapy if directed
Grapefruit or grapefruit juice if it interacts with medications
guidelines: Follow the oncology team's specific dietary recommendations during treatment
Eat small, frequent meals if appetite is poor or nausea is present
Gradually increase fiber intake after treatment as tolerated
Maintain adequate protein for healing and recovery
Discuss any supplements with the oncology team before use
Work with a dietitian experienced in oncology nutrition

Loss of consciousness
Severe allergic reaction to treatment
